INTRODUCTION

i OCCASION OF THE BOOK After his return to Africa and before his priestly ordination (391), probably in the year 390, Saint Augustine wrote the book De vera religione, to attract one of his best friends to Catholicism: the wealthy Romanianus, already known to those familiar with the works of the Saint, published by the B. A. C. Romanianus had been seduced by the prestige of the young professor of Tagaste to the Manichean sect; But, upon his conversion to the Catholic faith, one of his first desires as a neophyte was to recover for the truth the noble soul of his former benefactor and compatriot. Since Casiciaco's retirement he had promised to send him some treatise on the true religion at a later date 1. In a letter written in the year 390 he already announced the prompt sending of the work: "I have written something about the Catholic religion..., which I want to send to you before my arrival" 2. And he ended with this beautiful exhortation: "Leaving, then, the care of secular things, let us seek the real and true goods; let us take flight over the riches of the earth. Well, even in the abundance of honey, it is no wonder that the little bee has wings, because it imprisons and kills the one that adheres to it: Nam et in melliscopia 3 non frustra pennas habet apicula: necat enim haerentem". Later, around the year 395, in a written letter to Paulinus of Ñola and sent to Romanianus, who was going to Italy on business, he said: "Bearer of édta a Contra academics, II, 3: Cum tibí aliquam inter nos disputatlonem de religione misero, vel cum ptaesens tecum tumba coníulero." Epist. 15, 1. H-, 33, 8i2 ' IWd.

Your Excellency is a very dear and very familiar friend of mine since adolescence. His name is written in the book about the religion that your holiness, as indicated in the letter, is reading with great pleasure." In fact, Saint Paulinus had received through Saint Alypius five volumes of the first books of Saint Augustine, and among them the De vera religione. They all formed what he calls "the Pentateuch against the Manichaeans." In order to see the impression produced by the first works of Saint Augustine, I translate a fragment of the cited ^aita, when he was still renewing himself with the gift of Tagaste's friend: "The charity of Christ, which urges us and, even when we are absent, binds us in the unity of faith, has inspired me with confidence to write to you, overcoming all qualms: it has been infused in me through the writings, which, copious in streams of scholastic erudition, rich in divine honeycombs, medicinal and comforting for my seasoning, I possess in the five books that through We have received from our blessed and venerable bishop Alypius, not only for our instruction, but also for the benefit of the Church of many cities. Now I'm reading them; I delight in them. They offer me, not the perishable delicacy, but that which produces the substance of eternal life through our faith, with which we are incorporated into Jesus Christ... Oh true salt of the earth, which season our hearts so that they are not corrupted by the love of the world! Oh torch; worthily placed on the candelabra of the Church, which generously pours out from the seven arms, for the Catholic peoples, the light nourished with the anointing of joy! You dispel the dense darkness of heresies and with the splendor of your victorious word you shed the light of truth into the confusion of darkness. You see, oh brother of heart, admirable and worthy of being received in Christ, how familiarly I know you, what admiration and amazement I feel for you, with how much love I embrace you, I who every day enjoy the conversation of your books and receive the breath of your mouth! For I have rightly called your mouth a pipe of living water and a vein of the eternal fountain, because Christ has become a fountain in you of water that springs up to everlasting life. My soul thirsts for you with the desire for that water, and my land has longed to be intoxicated with the abundance of your flow" 5.

This impression of Saint Paulinus, one of the most conspicuous and literate characters of that time, reveals the healthy effects caused by reading the books of Si? n Augustine, whose genius began to produce joyful astonishment in

the Catholics and panic in the adversaries. Surely, the "Anti-Manichean Pentateuch" included, in addition to the book Of True Religion, the two De Genesi contra rtianichaeos and the De moribus Ecclesiae catholicae et de moribus manichaeorum, also written before he was ordained as a priest (388-390). Without a doubt, one of the most savored for its juicy style and the abundance and fluidity of ideas is the first, which Father Portalié describes as "un petit chef de oeuvre d'apologie", a brief masterpiece of apology, not only against the Manichaeans, but also against the infidels. The Catholic writer and thinker of vast syntheses and brilliant explorations pours his ideas into it with a warm and essential style. It is seen that Saint Augustine, still a simple layman, is taking intimate possession of Christianity and exploring the great themes of religious culture. One of the characters that enhance this book is the robustness and fullness of ideas, the solidity of its architecture. Its parts are assembled with a connection of great style. The Saint Augustine of the best times, with the admirable elasticity of his spirit, with the immense strength of his humanity, with the multiple radiation of his gaze; the ascetic and contemplative, the warrior and polemicist with a steely claw, the religious genius, Gothic and Romanesque at the same time, with the greatest thrust of Christianity, reflects his physiognomy in the smoothness of the pages of the book, which today we offer in translation to the Spanish public. Although it belongs to the cycle of anti-Manichean controversy, because it is built with the great metaphysical, religious and historical principles, it offers a Catholic and universal horizon; and his ideas enjoy the same freshness and vigor as in his time. They form a walled enclosure against an army of errors that in all ages strive to invade the mansion. of the truth of Christ. Let us not believe that Manichaeism is definitively defeated in the minds of many of our contemporaries. On the ruins of ancient errors, like a new basilica, trampling the remains of P-igan temples, the architectural genius of Saint Augustine elevates the Christian mass of his thought, with the triumphant lordship of history. Thus, pagan and profane stones serve God in their own way and old errors forever testify to the truth of the Catholic saying: It is appropriate that there be heresies.

The danger of many controversies lies in the predominance of the negative and circumstantial, which passes over time; but Saint Augustine triumphs over heresies with the positivity and strength of his genius. Also in this book we are shown 'Dict.
OF THE TRUE RELIGION

as a generous sower of ideas, deserving of high esteem for Catholic culture. Mr. Poujoulat makes this judgment: "The book Of True Religion is a vast view of genius on Christian revelation, where eloquence frequently sheds its vivid and brilliant colors: a true unction penetrates us and we feel the bowels of Saint Augustine being moved in it. In its rapidity, this book is a masterpiece from which philosophers and theologians can draw ideas in abundance. In its effort to tear the Manichaeans from the bonds of matter, of the corporeal world that dominated their understandings and held and imprisoned them as if in a narrow and dark dungeon, Augustine helps us ourselves to shake off the yoke of the senses, to transcend in a certain way the wall of this world that the passions raise between God and us, and behind which7 the luminous horizons of spiritualism extend." Antonio Arnauld expressed his admiration in these terms: "Who will not be amazed that, having so recently acquired knowledge of the mysteries of the Christian religion, and having no other quality in the Church than that of a simple believer, he was able to speak in such a noble and elevated manner of that divine religion, which God himself came to establish on earth, and to form such an excellent idea of its eminence and greatness, that one can hardly follow with the eye the flight of this eagle, penetrate the solidity of its admirable reasons and contemplate the sublime truths that it proposes, without being fainted in the sight of such a resplendent light?" And P. Batiffol writes: "Composed between 389 and 391, shortly before the book De utilitate credendi, the De vera reügione is a treatise on the rational knowledge of God, a demonstration of his existence against the Pyrrhonians and the pagans, a development of this thesis: reason can rise from the visible to the invisible and from the present to the eternal independently of authority and prior to it." The book contains all this, but in its most deep inside also contains a philosophy of religion and a defense of the bases of Christianity. Remember that it was written to attract a Manichaean to the Catholic faith and that Manichaeism constitutes an amalgam of metaphysical and religious conceptions. With the doctrine of the two coeternal and antagonistic principles it splits the unity of the cosmos and that of the divine plan.

in the economy of man's salvation. With particular effort, he exaggerates the disagreement of the two Testaments, without the possibility of harmony and concord. It also breaks the unity of history, since the present and the past lack an internal and pedagogical link, a sacred and primordial intention, which illuminates the process of events in the old and new world. The new appears without any point of support in the old, because prophecy becomes impossible and chaos prevails against order. There are no messianic times, and Christ appears as a solitary island in the dark immensity of the centuries. The essential corruption of man makes incarnation impossible, and the Son of God took on a fantastic body. Therefore Jesus is an apparent redeemer, without a deep connection with old or new humanity. As can be seen, the disciples of Manes undermine the eternal foundations of Christianity, starting with its monotheistic conception; and the neophyte of Tagaste was forced to work on the same ground as the foundations, seeking their support and firmness, not only in the order of ideas, but in that of historical facts, whose appearance and development is indubitable. From this fundamental and anti-Manichean position, where metaphysics, religion and history enter, one can glimpse the interior unity and architectural solidity of the book we analyze, and which can serve very well as a frontispiece to the collection of booklets that make up volume IV of his works. II OUR RELIGATION WITH GOD "Religet ergo nos religio omnipotenh Deo- religeznos religion with the almighty God, because between our mind, with which we know Him as Father, and the truth, that is, the inner light with which we understand, there is no creature interposed" 1. These brief words of Saint Augustine summarize a long thought of his, a primordial fact of the rational creature: the connection with God through a superior light. Let us ignore here the true etymological origin of the word religio, derived at the same time from relegere, religare and reelújere. There is no shortage of scholars who still admit the derivation pointed out here by Saint Augustine 2. We are interested here in the fact that the word religare and its derived religion imply. For the Holy Doctor, the spirit is not closed in itself, without openings or links with the real, but in contact with a triple realm of values: inferior, equal and superior. Value of values ​​is God, with whom it has an original and primordial relationship. The ideas that he summarizes in the book about true religion allude to a basic doctrine in it: that of truth. But the doctrine of truth is the doctrine of the religation of man with God, and therefore a metaphysical foundation of religion. Knowing the inner and higher light of truth is a conjunctive act with God. Therefore, the discovery of the intelligible world marks the beginning of religious metaphysics and the conversion of Saint Augustine, which can be defined as a curious case of spiritual heliotropism of his genius. He then turned toward the divine, reflected in the pure realm of eternal truths. Saint Augustine recounts that episode with a rare emotion of extraordinary adventure or great discovery, like the arrival and first vision of a fortunate island. It is beneficial to contemplate the spectacles of the universe: the starry sky, the whiteness of the light, the course of the sun and the moon, the diversity of the seasons, the fertility and beauty of the plants. The sensible world is captured by a sensitive perception, which indicates a higher degree of being: the one who feels is superior to the sensed. Man occupies a place superior to the visible world, and, although some animals surpass him in the perfection of the senses, he surpasses all with his intelligence, which is a communicating organ with an intelligible world. Sensitivity itself is subject to the judgment of reason, which is an indication of the superiority of the latter over the former. The judge is superior to the case tried. But the sensible world is linked to the intelligible, and in this aspect it forms a jurisdictional parcel of the same intelligence. Numbers order and illuminate material realities, and wisdom shines in all things, coming out to meet man to direct him in his efforts for ascension. As the senses have their own kingdom, which is of this world, reason has that of intelligible objects, v. gr., the concepts of number, unity, equality, wisdom, good and evil, and that of axioms or intelligible laws, such as those of numbers or mathematics, those of beauty or aesthetics, those of truth or logic and moral laws or ethics. The moral world offers our eyes blackness and darkness that can hardly be reduced to clarity with the light of pure reason. How in a cosmos where so much order reigns has disorder entered, what is that of human history? Who has unleashed upon the earth the furious wind of evils, which continually buffets us? The Manichaeans easily resolved the question: everything good comes from a good beginning; everything bad, from a bad beginning. The universe is not a universe, or a totality of beings under the lordship of a sovereign. Two lords rule in the world, two souls in men, two hostile and irreconcilable sides everywhere, The yes and the no war among themselves without the possibility of concord 1. The unfortunate balance of terrestrial happiness gave the sectarians of Manes argument for their doctrine. Saint Augustine, before his conversion to Christianity, had opposed dualism to the new ontology that is summarized in this book, affirming the supremacy of good and the slavery of evil to it, the essential goodness of the creature, without metaphysical defectibility, the explanation of the origin of evil as a defective movement of free will and, as a conclusion, the plurality of religions. The fundamental theses of his metaphysical optimism are reproduced here: all beings are good, even those who become evil and vitiated. Vice and evil sing of the goodness of the universe and the unity of divine government. Good cannot be evicted from any creature, no matter how evil. "All things are good that are damaged or corrupted; and they are destroyed because they are not perfect goods. Therefore, because they are good, they come from God; because they are not extremely good, they are not God. Therefore, the only good that cannot be corrupted is God. The rest come from Him, and can themselves be ruined, because of His harvest they are nothing, and through Him in part they are not corrupted and in part those that are corrupted are restored to their good." 2. Evil is the tendency to non-being, the deprivation of good, and when it lies in free will, it is called sin, which is essentially voluntary, so that it is not a sin if it is not committed with the will, as the wise and the ignorant agree. 4. Free will, as a creative force of the higher kingdom of values, is inserted in the fundamental questions of religious philosophy. Freedom belongs to the very heart of the religious act, because religion, in its subjective sense, is the liberal service of God, or what Saint Augustine calls liberáliter Deo serveré5. Serving God freely is the essential mission and destiny of the rational creature. This is all the more understood since divine service or worship itself is love, and to spiritual love the freedom of the lover is essential: Such enim servos suos meliores esse Deus iudicavit, si ei serverent liberáliter: quod nullo moda fieri posset si non volúntate, sed necessitate serverent e. If the service of God constitutes the glory and crown of the universe, freedom is an essential and decisive element in the destiny of rational beings. The order of love—orio amoris—means the exalted manifestation of the glory of God and the ultimate reward of free wills. But freedom can abandon the order of love and throw itself into disorder. With this terrible faculty, man was created to do good, but with the power to sin or rise up against the established order. Evil does not have its roots, as the Manichaeans wanted, in a chaotic matter, nor even in sensuality, but in voluntary and guilty decision. Sin is a voluntary defect with which man deviates from his principle to enjoy inferior goods inordinately 7. Analyzing the essence of sin, as aversion to God and conversion to inferior goods, we discover two immediate effects: as an aversive movement, it brings a defection or general weakening of the human being, who loses the support of the absolute and the firm. The creature, upon separating itself from God, feels moved in the deepest foundations of its being. "The soul decays, then, when it consents to evil, and, for this reason, its deterioration in the being and value that it previously had, when it remained united to virtue, begins; and the more it deteriorates, the more it deviates from the sovereign Being to unite with the lowest Being, with which it itself suffers a decrease. When the fullness of time arrived, God's mercy shined and a new historical period dawned with the appearance of Christ as the driving center of human destinies. He brought a "new form of religation with God, that is, a new type of life and religious existence, which will never expire." Once the old slavery was over, came the era of libertact, in which man had to be persuaded of the value of his will. Saint Augustine defines and qualifies the Christian era as one of freedom. A new form of divine service was only possible on condition of entering into conflict and destroying the power of evil, which constituted a spiritual kingdom antagonistic to that of God. Christ freed man from the dark power of evil, from the oppression of the law and from the fear of divine wrath, which darkened the souls of the servants of the old Covenant. The new type of humanity, created by the grace of the divine Liberator, surpasses the old, because it is freer and works by resources superior to that of earthly rewards. The old law, as an unbearable burden, made the free flight of the soul to God difficult or impossible. Christ abolished violence and terror; He did nothing by force, but with suasorio 2and attractive art: Nihií cgit vi, sed omnia suadendo et monendo. The new religion is based on interior freedom. The destiny of primitive man and that of the man rescued by Christ coincide exactly: liberaliter will serve Deo. But the Son of God does not shine with the terrible evidence of the iftyos and thunder of Sinai, but gently attracts men to unite them with Him. He deploys the same thaumaturgic power with parsimony and discretion, since he does not want to overwhelm souls, but to win them with love. Theirs will not form a warrior phalanx, but a flock of sheep and lambs in the midst of the wolves of the world. The freedom of love constitutes the wonderful contribution of the religion of Jesus. Man is called to an arduous undertaking, beyond his natural forces, with the support and grace of the Liberator, who presented himself as the only free one among men, as the Master and the living exemplar, inviting self-renunciation and honors, carnal pleasures, earthly possessions, and, at the same time, embraced contumelias, injuries, pain and death.

But, within the superiority of the ideal, Christianity will retain a similarity of structure with the ancient religion, since both the Mosaic people, engendered by the fear of the law (populus timore constrictus tempore servitutis in veteri lege), and the Christian people, born from the Gospel or the law of love, possess a sacramental economy, which serves as a religious bond between men. The ancient sacraments were given to Hespertar the "Church of grace, sung by the prophets." And when grace came, the same Wisdom of God, assuming a man, by whom we were called to freedom, instituted a few most salubrious sacraments, which contained the members of the society of the Christian people, that is, the free multitude under the one God. But are not many of the 'bears imposed on the Hebrew people, that is, on a popular mass subjected by fear of the one God, obligatory? and they have been left for the exercise of faith and interpretation. Thus now they do not slavishly oblige us4 and are useful for the liberal exercise of our soul." The diversity of economy does not favor the dualistic error of the Manichaeans, but rather manifests the intimate freedom of God in the distribution of his gifts. Divine sovereignty does not have to be tied to the regulating principles of our miserable reason, nor are the arcana of its will patent to us. A father of a family can well subject some to a regime of severity and, when he deems appropriate, take on others to the degree sublime freedom of his adopted children. The art of medicine is also subordinated to this prudence and peculiar adaptation 5. The sacramental system of the Christian religion is well adjusted to the nature of man, who cannot reach the content of the revelation of Christ by the path of philosophical speculation, but by the humble path of the sacraments. Its vitality and resistance to the most adverse currents of ideas and revolutions, its racial purity and its continuity throughout the centuries, make Israel not only a phenomenon, but a "noumenon of history", as Berdiaeff says; that is, a fact that reveals the essence of human events and destinies. "From any materialist or positivist historical point of view, this people should have disappeared long ago" 3. Only Christianity has glimpsed the secret of its destiny and predestination. The Hebrews are our booksellers, Saint Augustine would say; In the writing of Israel the library of the Christians was kept, or the prelude to the Gospel with the law and prophecy *. Thus it turns out, in a certain way, that the Hebrew people are not only the people of God, but also the people of Christ, because they carry the banner5 of messianic hopes in the procession of the centuries. The foundations of Christianity lie in Israel. From its ancient depths emerges the Root of Jesse, the Sapling of the new times, Jesus. This personality dominates all times with so much brilliance and evidence that it is necessary to close your eyes to not see it. Saint Augustine distinguishes in Christ three aspects that reveal his historical plenitude, which is not seen in any other religious figure: what he calls anteriora Chnsti, Christus and posteriora Christi. The entire countenance of Jesus is formed by what precedes Him, His person and what is derived from His influence. That is, Israel, which precedes him with the torment of the perpetual desire for a messianic future or the hope of the kingdom of God on earth; the real presence of Jesus in flesh on earth, to deposit in it the germ of a spiritual renewal that will change the face of the world; the Church, which receives its message and, as its mysterious body, prolongs its existence and its life between the persecutions of men and the consolations of God. Here is the historical trinity, which, imitating the divine, apparently offers three organs of epiphany, three different persons, but a single substance: Christ. Prophecy and history give expression to the physiognomy of the Redeemer. It could equally be said: prophecy, the real presence and history constitute the reliable proofs of the true religion, which is constantly alluded to in the apology of Saint Augustine. Now the phrase that we translated at the end of the previous chapter, referring to the development of the ages of man, will be better understood. The first age or spiritual childhood must

develop in the lap of tasty and profitable history: in uberibus utilis historiae, quae nutrit exemplis •.7 According to Saint Augustine, there is a "historia oognitio", of great significance in the pedagogy and ethics of man. History is the blessed and earthly bread with which Mother Church forms Christian intelligence in its first steps. In ancient catechesis, the instruction of aspirants to baptism began with the narratio, the narration of the works of God, referred to in the books of the Old Testament until reaching the times of the Church 8. The narration was the link of prophecy, of reality and history, or of the history of Israel, of the history of Christ and of the history of the Church. Firstly it was the parade of the Hebrew people with their providential destiny, miracle of the centuries; Then came the episodes of the temporal life of Jesus, and, finally, the new era of the world under the sign of grace. Ancient history is Christian prophecy, and its events, although they have their own subsistence, anticipate the realities of new times. These are not myths, but caryatids of the glorious Portico of the new Alliance. They are "factum et mysterium", as Saint Augustine would say, milestones of history and at the same time arcane hieroglyphs for the future world. Christ is the true noumenon of ancient history, "the substance of the people of Israel", as he would say, latent under the phenomena of its vital process throughout the centuries. That is why the concord and parallelism of both Testaments was the subject of assiduous Augustinian meditation against the arbitrary interpretation of Manichean dualism. Christ gives unity and similarity of structure to old and new history, lending decorum and order to its events and filling the course of waiting times with his presence. "In the six ages in which the course of the world is divided, Christ never ceased to be preached: in the five he is foretold by the prophets, in the sixth he is preached by the Gospel" 9. Therefore, the Messiah was the sweet goal of Saint Augustine's exegetical research: "When I eagerly go through the Scriptures with the sweat of our condemnation, openly or enigmatically, Christ meets me in all those books. The expression in se animas errantes divina commovebat auctoritas, alludes to a deep commotion caused by the power and goodness of the Wonderworker. The miracle, at the same time testimonium maestatis and testimonium bonitotis, works like a stone thrown into the stillness of a backwater, stirring the silt that sleeps in the lazy bed of the fins, stabilized in a way of living. For the renewal of religious consciousness, a vigorous reflex movement, an unfolding, is necessary through a catastrophe of a spiritual nature. Such was the work of Jesus: he deeply moved the human soul with his power and mercy, gaining sympathy and authority to put his healing hands on sick humans. Among the components, then, of Christ's authority is the mirum, which produces amazement, the glimpse of a transcendent power in prodigious works, whose presence produces a feeling of annihilation or humility in the creature. But this feeling, this horror honoris, due to the majestic, the extrapotent and divine, is tempered by the tremor amoris, by the love towards the beneficent Wonderworker, by a movement of sympathy and rapprochement, whose effect is unreserved surrender, fides, faith. By faith, the believer places himself in the hands of the divine Benefactor and accepts the medicine of his complete healing. Thus he conquered and transformed the multitude of followers and believers, forming with them the germ of the Church, continuing its action throughout the centuries. From the above it follows that the Christian religion is a religion of authority and not of reason. Although it would be better to say that it is a religion of authority and reason, because faith and intelligence guide the secret of Christianity. Furthermore: it is the only reasonable religion, because Christ is the only reason for the world and history, the only mediator capable of uniting men with God. He is also, through his miracles, through his life and his doctrine, the strongest rational support of Christianity. Saint Augustine excludes the rationalist or illuminist conception of religion, which was the one that had seduced his mind during his stay in the sect of Manes. The authority of Christ is strengthened by two things: partim miraculis, partim multitudine. The reason of the multitude, the social force, or in more concrete terms, the Church, develops a great plastic and attractive power in the earthly constitution of the kingdom of God.

In the moral aspect, Saint Augustine highlights "the excellent holiness and inexhaustible fruitfulness of the Church in all goods." In the beautiful apostrophe to the Catholic Church, mother of wisdom, he lists part of them: the worship of God, public and universal, in spirit and truth, clean of all errors; love of neighbor and "the medicine for the various diseases that souls suffer from their sins"; the pedagogical system of man's formation adjusts to all ages and conditions; the elevation of women, freeing them from the servitude of men; the sanctity, reverence and internal discipline of marriage; the general brotherhood of men, reinforcing their natural bonds; the relations between the subjects and the supreme authority; those of some men with others; the family, civil, national and international order; the education of the human race for a type of supernatural existence, which 'perfects and ennobles: these are undeniable fruits that the Church has brought to the world, and which Saint Augustine mentions in the aforementioned apostrophe'. Christianity possesses the perfect ideal of morality, the means to fulfill it and those who strictly observe it: -> "No wonder you keep the divine precepts throughout the world, how long and wide it extends. No wonder you have so many who receive pilgrims, so many who fulfill their obligations, so many merciful, so many learned, so many chaste, so many saints, so many so inflamed with the love of God, that, maintaining the utmost continence and contempt unspeakable of the world, they are delighted by the same solitude" 8. Saint Augustine also lists various elevated forms of holiness and parades the most egregious exemplars, such as the anchorites, of prodigious asceticism and the highest contemplative life, "most blessed in the contemplation of the beauty of God, which can only be perceived with the understandings of the saints"; the Cenobites, "who offer to God, as the gift that is most pleasing to Him, a life full of charity and devotion to the Lord, with whose grace they persevere in it"; and they are interested in the work of their hands for the poor, ensuring that "what is left over does not remain in their power, to the extent that they send loaded ships to the lands where there are poor people"; religious with an angelic life, who serve God with fervor and purity of customs and live by the work of their hands; ecclesiastics of resplendent examples of virtue, despite living among the vices of the

The city of God is not immune to this conflict and bitter experience: it knows that the roots of evil undermine the spirit of man and strive to suffocate the energies of good; But precisely in the heart of these conflicts and contradictions, God's victory shines with greater decorum. At this point it is worth clarifying an opinion by Father Ildefonso Herwegen, expressed in his acutelB essay entitled Antike, Germanentum und Christentum. Since true religion is the norm of every good and happy life, with which a single God is honored and with very sincere piety is recognized as the principle of all beings, which in Him have their origin and from Him receive the virtue of their development and perfection, the error of the people who wanted to venerate many gods, instead of the one and true one, Lord of all, is very clearly seen, because their wise men, called philosophers, had divergent doctrines and common temples. For their discordant way of thinking about the nature of the gods was not hidden from both the people and the priests, because they did not shy away from publicly expressing their opinions, striving to persuade others if they could; Despite this, together with their followers, divided among themselves by diverse and contrary opinions, without prohibition from anyone, they went to the temples. It is not intended now to declare which of them came closest to the truth; But it appears quite clear, in my opinion, that they publicly embraced some religious beliefs, in accordance with popular sentiment, and privately maintained others contrary to the knowledge of the same people.

When, then, we inquire who made them, let us look for Him who is beautiful among all, for all beauty is derived from Him. And who is this, but the one God, the one truth, the health of all things, the first and sovereign essence, from which comes everything that is insofar as it has being, because everything that is, as such, is good? 22. After God, death does not come. God did not make death nor does he take pleasure in the destruction of the living; Because it is the highest essence, it gives being to everything that is, from which it receives the name essence. But death precipitates into non-being everything that dies, as soon as it dies. For if mortal or corruptible things entirely lost their being, they would become nothing; but as long as their being is diminished, they die; or put more briefly, the more they die the less they are. Thus, every body is less than any life, because whatever form it has left, it lasts in being through life, whether it is the one that governs every animated being, or the one that directs the nature of the universe. Therefore the body is more subject to death and, therefore, closer to nothingness. Therefore, the living being that abandons God through bodily enjoyment3 tends toward nothingness, and this is malice or foolishness.

The people desired riches with pernicious desire, as satellites of delights: He wanted to be poor. They perished for honors and commands: He did not allow them to make him king. They valued carnal offspring as a treasure: He did not seek marriage or children. With great pride they avoided outrages: He endured all kinds of them. They considered insults unbearable; Well, what greater injustice than the just and the innocent being condemned? They execrated bodily pain: He was scourged and tormented. They were afraid to die: He was sentenced to death. They considered the cross as the most ignominious type of death: He was crucified. With his detachment he lowered the value of things, whose greed was the cause of our bad life. With his passion he removed everything that diverted us, with the desire to avoid it, from the study of the truth. For no sin can be committed except by desiring the things He hated or avoiding the things He suffered. 32. His entire earthly life, as a man, whose nature he deigned to take, was the discipline of customs. And with his resurrection from the dead he showed well that nothing perishes from human nature, because God saves everything, and how all things serve their Creator, now for revenge of sins, now for the liberation of man, and how easily the body serves the soul if it submits to God. When this is done, not only is no substance evil, because it is an impossible thing, but it is not even affected by the evil that could have come from sin and its revenge. Such is the natural discipline, worthy of full faith for poorly instructed Christians, and for the learned, cleansed of all error. I do not admit that there is anyone among the deniers of divine worship who is either not a slave to carnal delights, or has a vain estimate of its power, or does not lose his senses with attractions and spectacles. Thus, without noticing it, they go out of their way for temporal goods, hoping to find happiness in them. But, necessarily, whether he likes it or not, man is a servant of the things in which each person places happiness. For wherever they lead him, he follows them, and looks with suspicion at the One who can take them away from him. And a fiery storm and a despicable little animal can snatch them away. In short, omitting the innumerable adversities, time necessarily takes with it everything transitory. Since this world is the theater of all temporal things, those who want to shake off the yoke of every religious cult so as not to serve are enslaved to everything in it. 70. Notwithstanding this, although they lie miserably in the lower extremity, accepting the sovereignty of guilty vices, either by lightness, or by pride or curiosity, or by two of them, or by all three, while they are in the stage of the present life, they can attack them and overcome them, if they first submit by faith to what they cannot yet understand and separate themselves from the world, since everything that is in it, according to the divine sentence, is lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes and ambition of the world. This is how those three vices are characterized, since the concupiscence of the flesh means lovers of the lowest pleasure; the lust of the eyes, to the curious, and the ambition of the century, to the proud. 71. Human Truth also showed us the triple temptation that must be avoided. Tell these stones to become bread, says the tempter. But He, the only and sovereign Teacher, answers him: Man does not live by bread alone, he lives by every word that comes from God. Thus he taught us that the appetite for pleasure must be tamed, so that not even hunger must be yielded to. But perhaps he who was previously conquered by carnal delight could be seduced with the pageantry of temporal domination; All the kingdoms of the world were shown to him, and it was said to him: I will give you everything if you worship me by prostrating yourself. But he received this reply: You will worship the Lord, your God, and Him only you will serve. Thus pride was trampled.

Then came the last temptation of curiosity, as the tempter spurred him to rush from the top of the temple, with the flattery of a new experience. But he was not defeated here either, and he responded in a way that we understood was not necessary, to know God, any industry aimed at exploring the divine: Do not tempt the Lord, your God, he told him. Let us also believe that this is the will of the best angels and the most excellent ministers of God: that we worship with them the Lord, whose contemplation beatifies them. 29. The Ages of Man (XXVI, 49).—The ancient apologists faced the pagan objection to the late appearance of Christianity. Being a message of health, how was it offered to the human race so late? This objection raised the problem of the evolutionary process of history. The old is a preparation for the new. A slowly developed economy anticipated the coming of the Son of God on earth, the messianic times, which are of plenitude and maturity. These are not two antagonistic manifestations or two adverse religious principles, one of which undoes the work of the other, as the Manichaeans fantasized, opposing the Old and the New Testament, but rather a perfect unity of plan, a theophanic process, from less to more, whose development can be compared with the ages of man. Already in Saint Irenaeus the doctrine of the ages of history is outlined with these apologetic purposes. Humanity has its childhood, its times of inexperience and consecutive development. And God's truth has accommodated this weakness. "It was necessary that man be created, and after being created he should grow, and with his growth he should gain strength, and being strengthened he should multiply, and by multiplying he should become powerful, and that by his strength he should be glorified, and glorified should see God" (Adver. haer., IV, c. 38, 1-3). The historical process of humanity from its fall to its redemption enriched the experience of human misery. On the other hand, ancient theophanies prepared it for the definitive appearance of God on earth. The same for Saint Irenaeus as for Saint Augustine, two things stand out in the ancient economy: the slow process towards an increasingly perfect religious ideal, whose unity of intention does not allow division, and the constant intervention of God in human events. But this process does not nullify the transcendence of Christianity nor its impression of a great novelty in history. Cf. K. PüüMM: Ckristentum ais Neuheitserlebnis. Freiburg i. With the empire of ghosts, the lower psyche, detached from the sovereignty of the spirit, becomes bossy, enslaving man. The evocation of images does not obey the restraint of the rational will, but rather develops according to its own autonomous laws, weakening the exercise of reasoning and creating all kinds of idolatry at the service of the passions. One of the profound aspects of Christ's redemption is liberation from internal idolatry. Faith redeems us from the slavery of our ghosts and makes us live in a luminous world, where things occupy their true place. On the contrary, idolatry is the inversion of all ontological values. Saint Augustine always insists on placing the source of all religious impiety in intimate idolatry, or slavery and servitude to the ghosts, which the passions have created for their own bait and delight. 58. This was the reason that moved him to read the holy Scriptures, because he knew from his holy mother that they contained true wisdom; but his vanity was offended by the simplicity and simplicity of his style, and his puffiness and arrogance refused to accept the sacrifice of humility that they imposed on the understanding. MANÍ: HIS LIFE, WORKS AND DISCIPLES Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, was born in Babylon, of Persian parents, in the year 215 or 216. Babylon was then the seat of the most intense religious syncretism; There existed there a variegated mixture of the most conflicting religious ideas, such as Christian, Jewish, Gnostic, Mazdeist and Buddhist ideas. The founder of the Manichean sect does not appear on the scene as an innovator, since, as he said, the truth is one and he had his apostles before him, like Buddha. Zoroaster and Christ. Mani believed himself to be the Paraclete promised by Christ, with the highest hope of making a synthesis of the three doctrines and of announcing or preaching this gospel in all regions and in all languages, as a universal religion. In order to establish his doctrines well and remove from them as much as possible the danger of falsification by the disciples in oral dissemination, Manes decided to put them in writing. In accordance with the awareness he had of his mission, he gave himself body and soul to the study of religious documents. The greatest difficulty he had to overcome at this point was the knowledge of the documents of the Buddhist religion, and he heroically overcame it by moving to India, where he founded a community before his return to Persia. In order to make it easier to spread his doctrines in Persia, he made all kinds of attempts to win the favor of the court. The first time he met King Shapur I, for whom he wrote a book in Persian that contained his religious thoughts, he did not come away badly impressed from the interview. But the magicians soon had a very hostile tendency prevail at the court, which forced him to flee again to India. Upon the death of Shapur I he believed the opportunity to return to Persia had arrived. During Humuzd's brief reign he gained favor at court. But very soon, in the reign of Bahram, his successor, such favo/, was changed " Sloiia (tille religloni diretta da Pietro Tacchi Venturi: 11 mar nlclmi¡>iuu, pp 243-244.

Captured and defeated by Mani in an argument with the magicians of Mazdeism, he was sentenced to death and was beheaded, and his corpse was skinned, and, as a perpetual lesson, his skin, dissected17 and filled with straw, was hung in a public place (273-277). The fruit of the study of the religious documents of his time was the fruitful literary production of the founder of the Manichean sect. He wrote not only great didactic treatises, but also countless letters, which kept him in contact with the disciples he gained during his missionary wanderings. According to the Arab historian Al-Nadim, Mani composed seven books, one of them in Persian and the others in the Syriac language. The order that follows in the enumeration is as follows: the book of the Mysteries, the Giants, the Precepts, the one entitled Shapuraham, the book of Life, and the one entitled Farakmatija. Ab-Nadim's text, which has a gap here, does not give us the title of the announced seventh book. The index that Biruni gives, around the year 1000, of Mani's works, almost reproduces that of the author of the Fihrist. This historian says that he found in Hawarizim a volume of Manichean books that contained the following writings, in this order: the one entitled Farakmatija, that of the Giants, the Treasure of Life, the Sun of Certainty and Foundation, The Gospel, Shapuraham, a collection of letters from Mani and the book of the Mysteries. These indexes, according to critics, are the most complete and most credible of Mani's authentic writings. We must understand the Syriac language, in which the author of the Fihrist Mani wrote the first six works of his catalogue, not the classical language, but the Aramaic of Babylon and, speaking more precisely, the language of Suritan, that is, of the region of the Tigris and the lower Euphrates. What is known about each of these books? It was already said, when it came to the sources of Manichaean history, that of all the literary production of Manichaeism, only fragments and summaries of works were preserved, and that, furthermore, Mani's originals were considered lost forever; however, some idea can still be given of these books. In the book of the Mysteries it seems that it was about the relations between Judaism and Christianity, and especially the relations between the body and the soul.

The Book of the Giants, which seems, according to Alfaric's plausible hypothesis, to be identified with the Líber Capitulorum (book of principles), would surely be a synthesis of the essential doctrines (-z'cyXom) of Manichaeism. The one of the Precepts was

a Manichean Ethics, divided into two parts: one for the listeners and the other reserved for the chosen or perfect. Alfaric sees in this work what Saint Augustine mentions in the book De moribus manicha&orum, and which he partly analyzes. The Shapurakam is believed to be the work that Mani composed for the great king of the Persians Shapur I, in order to instruct him and win him over to the sect. Its content is eschatological. The book of Life or Treasure of life or simply the Treasure was known to Saint Augustine, of whom he quotes two fragments in his works, which is almost the only thing that remains of this treatise, and there were at least seven books. It described the struggle between the two kingdoms, that of darkness and that of light, and the role played by the third messenger and the Virgin of Light in the redemption of the divine elements, held captive by the aerial demons. The book that bears the title of Farmkmatija (IIf.ciua-sí(?) is, according to Alfaric, the Epistle that the Manichaeans call the Fundament, a summary of the entire doctrine of the religion of Mani. It is the writing that we know best, thanks to Saint Augustine, against whom he made a proper refutation and of which he transcribed important paragraphs. One finds there a description of the two eternal principles, of the original struggle between good and evil. of history. of man and the redemption, carried out by Christ, that is, a systematic exposition of the teachings of M-sni. The Gospel or Living Gospel, as it is called in many texts, preaches, according to Biruni, the true faith of Mani, and it is also said that, outside of it, everything is vanity and lies. These seven treatises are the capital works of the founder of the Manichean sect. He only had 1Sfifty-two in his hands. All of these letters have also been lost. The sect, for almost a millennium, remained strong and vigorous and managed, despite the persecutions to which it was subjected, to penetrate the East and the West. The penetration of the religion of Mani in Peru, in Central Asia and in the Roman Empire, was not only the work of the astonishing activity of the founder and of the disciples whom he won during his lifetime, but also of his successors, who, aware, like the master, of their very high mission, continued his work with incredible tenacity. Manichaeism took root in Persia until the 6th century, despite the tenacious persecution to which it was always the object of the Mazdeans. It was in the reign of Chosroas I when the coup de grace was given (531-570). After Mani's tragic end, many of the disciples, following the master's example, fled to the East, to the regions of the Oxus and the Hindukusch, where they were able to settle peacefully. They managed to have great influence in Chinese Turkestan, as they converted the khan of the Uyghurs (Mogolic-Turkish tribes), with his court, to the sect in 772, and later the entire kingdom. But this triumph of Manichaeism did not last long. In 840, the Uyghur Empire was broken by the Kirghiz, who destroyed the capital and imprisoned the Uyghur khan. The religion of Mani did not disappear, however, in the States that were established on the ruins of the Uyghur Empire, since some remained faithful to the doctrines of Mani. It is precisely there, in the regions inhabited by the Uyghurs, in Turpan, Russian Turkestan and Tun-Huang (cave temple area in the Chinese province of Kan-Su). where the Manichean texts of which we have already spoken were found, and which testify to the influence of the religion of Mani on the inhabitants of the country. But since the change of dynasty, the edicts of persecution against the Manichaean sect and other foreign sects begin and continue incessantly, until 1B the edict d.3 1370 gave the sect of Mani the final blow. It is known with certainty that within a few years of J«Iani's death, Manichaeism had infiltrated so much into the Roman Empire, especially in Africa (the land of choice for Maniaucism), that the proconsul of Africa denounced the sect to Diocletian, who decreed the penalty of fire against the leaders and that of beheading against its followers.

VII MANICHAEAN DOCTRINES: MANICHAEAN DOGMATICS A definitive exposition of Mani's system cannot yet be made today, since the publication of Mani's original documents discovered in Egypt will still take a few years. Consequently, the doctrinal construction of Manichaeism has to be based on other documents that history provides us, such as the polemical texts, the Turfan documents and the Coptic fragments already published by Schmidt. These documents are enough to definitively trace the main architectural lines of Mani's doctrinal conception. Only some points that will still remain obscure can be elucidated by the founder's own writings. Mani's mission, as he himself says, was not to flood a new doctrine, but to reduce to a synthesis the doctrines that other founders of religions had already announced. But, in fact, in carrying out this enterprise he is not eclectic, but profoundly modifies such doctrines 2l. Manichaeism is neither Buddhist, nor Christian, nor Zoroastrian, nor Gnostic doctrine; It is a systematization of elements of each of these doctrines, deeply transformed and deformed. MANICHEAN ETHICS The syntheses of Mani's ethics are the three seals indicated. By virtue of the seal of the mouth, the disciples of Mani are prohibited from putting anything impure into the mouth, nor from leaving it. Consequently, lies, blasphemies, apostasies, perjury and oaths are prohibited. They are also, and very severely, certain foods, such as, for example, meat and, in general, all animal products, since these, being creatures of demons, are essentially evil. Death makes the divine principle that it contained completely disappear from his body and he is transformed into a mass full of filth. Eggs lose their vital or divine elements when they are opened, and milk when it comes out of the animals. Only plant foods are authorized, such as rice, truffles, mushrooms, onions, garlic, leeks, melons, pepper, legumes and fruits. The fate of the chosen ones, after death, is immediate entry into the kingdom of light or paradise. The fate of the listeners is not so happy, since they are destined to remain in this world subject to the law of metempsychosis until they come to incarnate in the body of a saint or perfect person, which is their last stage, a prelude to redemption or definitive health. The fate that awaits sinners is hell, with its eternal and hopeless tortures. However, the definitive separation of the good and the bad, that is, of light and darkness, will take an uncountable number of centuries, for the return to their origin of the luminous eons, captive in the universe of matter. At the end of time the world will be the theater of a great catastrophe, which will be announced by a divine messenger. A universal fire will break out on the earth to purify and judge it. With this final act, the last particles of light still imprisoned in matter will be released and will rise to the sky, while matter will remain formless and motionless. Only the good principle will reign over the purified universe, without fearing any invasion of its opposite for all eternity *.

MANICHAEAN CHURCH: ORGANIZATION AND LITURGY The Manichaean religious society was hierarchically organized by two categories of adepts: that of the elect ("sons of the mystery") and that of the listeners ("sons of intelligence"). The first were the followers of the religion "Manichehme,

integral, and the others could be considered at his side, as adherents and coadjutors. Among the chosen ones there was a hierarchy: the supreme degree belonged to the teachers, who were twelve, and they were called by the nickname "the children of sweetness"; The second degree was seventy-two bishops, who were called "sons of science"; and inferior to these were the presbyters or "sons of wisdom" and the deacons. AND! supreme head of the hierarchy, known in the West by the title of prince, was chosen from among the teachers, and resided from the beginning in Babylon, and his authority was universally recognized. But various political circumstances and persecutions forced the Manichaeans to move their headquarters to Samarkand 25. Saint Augustine, in his book of heresies, mentions this hierarchy, which is similar to the Catholic one 2a. The Manichean Church had its sacramental rites, such as baptism and the Eucharist, reserved exclusively for the saints. What still remains a mystery is what elements constituted such rites. It is also conjectured that, on the occasion of the Eucharist, the saints frequently mixed truly nefarious practices. We still have fragmentary knowledge of their prayers, hymns and liturgical festivals. There is some news of a series of prayers that claim to have been inspired and prescribed by the Paraclete to his chosen ones and addressed to the Paraclete himself, to his angels and to the supreme God of light, and which had to be prayed accompanied by another similar series of prostrations. These prayers were followed by others that during the day, says Saint Augustine, were addressed to the sun and at night to the moon, if it appeared, and if not, to the northern part of the sky. Hymns from his liturgy are also known, which show a certain depth of religious meaning and perhaps even internal piety, along with a deep pessimistic feeling, given the sad condition of man and the world. These hymns are invocations to Jesus and his Paraclete in demand of help and help. The confession of sins was also a practice of the sect: the listeners kneeled next to the saints in a supplicating attitude, in order to receive the laying on of hands, a sensible sign of the forgiveness of their sins 2 '.

4. Let us see, then, in the light of reason, what the life of man should be. It is true that we all want to live a happy life, and there is no one who does not agree with this proposition even before finishing its statement. Happier, in my opinion, is not the one who does not possess what he loves, whatever the object of his love may be; nor does he who possesses what he loves, if it is harmful; nor is he who does not love what he has, even if it is very good. For he who burns with desire for what he cannot obtain, is himself his crucifixion; He who obtains what he should not love is fatally deceived, and he who does not desire what he should obtain is not healthy. In none of these states is the soul free from misery; and since misery and happiness cannot be together at the same time in man, that is why none of these are happy. There remains only a fourth situation, in which a happy life can occur, and it is that produced by the love and possession of the highest good of man. What is enjoyment, if not having the presence of what you love? No one without enjoying the highest good of man is happy; and he who enjoys it, can he not be? It is necessary, therefore, if we want to be happy, the presence in us of the highest good. 5. What is this supreme good of man? anyone who

7. What is the highest good of the body? Right reason forces us to recognize that it is that which communicates its greatest perfection and happiness. But nothing that gives life, vigor and strength is better and more excellent than the soul. The supreme good of the body is, therefore, neither pleasure, nor the lack of pain, nor strength, nor beauty, nor agility, nor anything corporeal, but only the soul. She is, in fact, the one who with her presence communicates to the body everything I just said, and, furthermore, life, which is better than everything. Therefore, the soul is not the supreme good of man, whether by this name the body and the soul are designated together, or the soul alone. Because if reason discovers that the highest good of the body is better than it and that which gives it vigor and life, whatever the meaning of the term man may be, either the body and the soul, or only the soul, there is a need to continue the investigation of the existence of something that is more excellent and better than the soul and that, if it adheres to it, elevates it to the perfection and happiness of which it is capable. This good, if discovered, will undoubtedly be, rightly and justly, the supreme good of man. 8. Now, if the body is the man, it is undeniable that the soul is his best good. 13. What rule of life does the Lord give us in his Gospel, and after Him the apostle Paul? The Manichaeans do not dare to condemn these Scriptures. May we hear with attention and respect, O Christ, what end or happiness You prescribe for us! Will it not be, without a doubt, the same one to whom you order us to turn with all the forces of love? You shall love, he says, the Lord your God. Tell me yet what is the measure of that love, because I fear that I will burn with the desire and love of my God more or less than is appropriate. You will love Him, He tells me, with all your heart; and this is still not enough. You will love him with all your soul. Even this is not enough yet. You will love him with all your mind. What more do you want? I would love even more if I didn't see that what lies beyond is nothingness. What does Paul add to this? We know that everything works together for the good of those who love God. Let him also tell us the measure of love. Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Is it affliction, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or the sword? We have heard what we should love and to what extent. This is the end of the direction and reference of all our thoughts. God is for us the sum of all goods, he is our supreme good. We should neither stay here nor go further: the first is dangerous, and the second, nothingness.

Love yourselves, I beg you, with the interest of a father, to consider with love and attention what the meaning of what we say is. Look and you will see that you are full of poverty and misery! Do we not reprove more strongly and severely than your sect what attributes to God qualities that are completely incompatible with his nature? Do we not correct the simplicity of those who understand the quoted passages of Scripture literally, or do we not laugh at their childish pertinacity? There are, furthermore, other points that you do not understand: that Catholic doctrine prohibits believing those who, more because of their studies and intelligence than because of years, have passed beyond age, let's say, spiritual childhood and are advancing in the knowledge of venerable wisdom. It is true madness, according to Catholic doctrine, to believe that God is contained in a place, even if it is infinite, and a crime to believe that He Himself or one of His parts moves and goes from one place to another. It also describes as impious and foolish to only imagine that it can undergo alteration or change in its nature or substance. It is true that there are infantile spirits among us who represent God as a human form and also believe that this is his being or reality, and that does not mean that it is a less abject and despicable opinion; But it is also true that there are many other spirits, very advanced in the knowledge of wisdom, who see with intelligence their inviolable and immutable greatness, transcending not only bodies, but intelligence itself. Age here is not years: it is prudence and wisdom. I know that within your sect there is no one who represents divinity as the form of a human body; but I am not unaware that there is no one to preserve it clean from human error. While those who are nursed like children by the Catholic Church, if the heretics do not steal them from us, each one develops according to his capacity and needs, and advances towards the age of the perfect man, and then towards the maturity and whiteness of wisdom, and finally arrives, to the extent of his will, to live a very happy life.

The path of happiness is the first and main precept of the Lord: You will love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your spirit, For lovers of God everything works together for good. This is why Saint Paul himself adds next; I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor powers, neither present nor future things, neither what is higher nor what is deeper, nor any creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, who is Christ our Lord. The more distant from God, not because of local distance, but because of the affection and desire for things inferior to Him, the more is his blindness and misery; love, on the contrary, turns it to God, love that eagerly desires that the soul be its slave, not equal to Him. Tenacity and diligence in seeking it will be the measure of its perfection and happiness, and docility in total and complete subjection to God will cause the most perfect freedom. The soul must, therefore, recognize that it is a simple creature, and see its Creator as he is, eternally subsisting in the inviolable and immutable nature of truth and wisdom, and confess that it may be subject to blindness and lies because of the very errors from which it so eagerly desires to be free. What, according to this, is the holy life, the life that is the itinerary of happiness, than the love of Virtue, Wisdom and Truth, but love with all the heart, with all the soul and with all the spirit? Will not holiness be the same as the perfect love of inviolable and invincible Virtue, of Wisdom into which ignorance and folly never penetrate, and of Truth that neither changes nor ever exists otherwise than it eternally is? This truth reveals the Father to us, as Jesus expresses it: No one comes to the Father except through me. Holiness unites us with Him. Fully penetrated by the spirit of holiness, we burn ourselves in the fullness and perfection of charity, which alone causes union and resemblance with God, rather than with the world, as these words of the Apostle signify: God predestined us in order to make us conformed to the image of his Son 1. 23. It is, then, charity that produces our resemblance to God; and thus, conformed and as if sealed with the seal of divine likeness and segregated or separated from the world, let us never mix again with the creatures, who must always be our slaves. This is the work of the Holy Spirit alone. Hope is never frustrated, says Saint Paul, because the charity of God has been spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been communicated to us. Our renewal by the Holy Spirit could not be carried out if He did not always remain the same in His integrity and immutability; which would also not be possible without being of the same substance or nature as God, which is immutability and, so to speak, invertibility itself. The creature, however (these are not my words, they are Saint Paul's), is a slave to vanity or lies. That which is subject to vanity cannot separate us from it nor unite us with the truth; This is the exclusive work of the Holy Spirit; It is not, therefore, a creature, because what exists is either God or a creature.

25. Since virtue is the path that leads to true happiness, its definition is none other than a perfect love of God. Its fourfold division expresses nothing more than several affections of the same love, and that is why I do not hesitate to define these four virtues (which hopefully have as much roots in the hearts as their names do in everyone's mouths) as different functions of love. Temperance is love that totally gives itself to the loved object; strength is the love that endures everything for the object of its loves; justice is "love that is solely the slave of its beloved and that exercises, therefore, lordship according to reason; and, finally, prudence is the love that with sagacity and wisdom chooses the means of defense against all kinds of obstacles. This love, we have said, is not love of any object, but love of God, that is, of the highest good, it adds wisdom and peace. For this reason, making the definitions more precise, it can be said that temperance is the love that is preserved whole and incorruptible to God alone; strength is the love that all

37. The attractions of bodies lie in what the corporeal senses perceive, and which some call sensitive; and it is the light that has primacy among them, since among the senses, which are at the service of the soul, sight is the preferred one; and this is also the reason for calling the sacred Scriptures visible to everything sensible. In the New Testament we are prohibited from loving him in this precept of the Apostle: Do not fix your attention on what is visible, but on what is invisible; for what is visible is temporary, but what is invisible is eternal. From this it follows that those who believe in the duty not only to love the sun and the moon, but also to worship them are not Christians. Does our sight see anything if it does not see the sun and the moon? Since it is forbidden to look at visible things, much more will anyone who wants to offer it to God pure and incorruptible have to withdraw from his love. I leave this now to deal with it more carefully and diligently elsewhere. My intention at present is not to talk about faith but about the life that deserves to achieve intelligence as much as one believes. Only God deserves our love; Everything else, everything sensible, on the contrary, is worthy of contempt and that we should only use it to the extent of the needs of life.

This is the rule of life that justice prescribes to the loving soul, which is in question: prompt service and with the best good will to the God of his loves, who is supreme good, supreme wisdom and supreme peace; and all other things, he rules and governs, part of them as subject to him and part as foreseeing that one day they will be so. This rule of life is confirmed, as we say, by the testimony of both Testaments. 45. Little will also be said about prudence, which is nothing other than the discovery of the object of our loves and our hatreds. It is enough for us to know that without it none of the above can be done well. It is characteristic of her to be vigilant and diligent so as not to be seduced, neither suddenly nor little by little; and that is why the Lord often repeats to us: Always be awake and walk while the light lasts, so that the darkness does not surprise you; and the same thing with Saint Paul: Don't you know that a little yeast is enough to infect the entire dough? Against this negligence and sleep of the spirit, which barely realizes the successive infiltration of the serpent's venom, these words of the prophet that are read in the Old Testament are very clear: He who despises small things will fall little by little. I am going very quickly, I cannot stop in extensive explanations of this most wise maxim; But, if this were my purpose, I would show the greatness and depth of these mysteries, which are the mockery of men as noble as they are sacrilegious, who do not fall little by little, but rather quickly, into the depths of the abyss.

48. Let the Lord speak to us about the second precept, who, when asked about the precepts of life, did not speak of a single one, knowing, as he did, that God is one thing and man another, and as different as is the distinction between the Creator and the creature, made in his image. The second precept: You shall love, it says, your neighbor as yourself. Your love for yourself will not be good if it is greater than the love you have for God. And the same thing that you do with yourself, do it with your neighbor, so that he may also love God with perfect love. Well, you don't have the same love for him as you do for yourself if you don't strive to guide him towards the good that you are aiming for; This is a good of such a nature that it does not decrease with the number of those who together with you tend to Him. These men without any swelling of pride, without any confusion or yellowish pallor, born of stubbornness and envy, but always modest, humble, long-suffering, offer God this life of perfect harmony and perpetual contemplation as a most gratifying gift of theirs. No one owns anything as their own nor is anyone else's burden. They engage in manual work, which provides them with what is necessary to nourish the body, without distracting the spirit and the thought of God. Once their work is finished, they hand it over to the deans (since each one commands ten religious), and they are neglectful of all material things, whether it refers to food, clothing, or everything that daily needs and health care require. The deans arrange everything with great care and promptly fulfill the demands of life and all the needs of the body, themselves giving an account of their administration to the one they call father. These fathers are not only most holy, but also most excellent in the science of the divine and of spirit elevated above all things; They look without any arrogance and with great concern for the good of those they call their favorite children, whom they command with their great authority and who are obeyed with a great will. 69. Do not believe, however, that the most holy customs of the Catholic Church do not exceed the narrow limits of those most holy souls whose life has earned me so much praise. How many bishops, priests, deacons, and ministers of the divine mysteries have I known who were most excellent and holy men, which is so difficult to see within human conversation and the whirlwind of life! Because their requests and care are not primarily for the healthy, but for the sick. They have to endure the vices of the people to cure them and tolerate pestilent wounds rather than heal them. It is very difficult in these circumstances to be holy and live a life of peace and tranquility of spirit. I will say it in a few words: these spend their lives where one learns to live, while those (the anchorites and cenobites) are where one truly lives.

There is, furthermore, in the Catholic Church another order of Christians who equally deserve my praise; I am referring to those who live in community, within cities, a Christian life very different from ordinary life. I myself knew in Milan a community of saints governed by a most holy and wise priest; In Rome I learned of many communities always governed by those who stood out most among them in gravity, prudence and science of the divine, and they lived together a life whose breath was Christian charity, holiness and freedom; and in order not to be each other's burden, they sustained themselves, according to the custom of the East and the example of Saint Paul the Apostle, by the work of their hands. The fasting of many was incredible: it was not limited to just one meal in the evening (a universal custom), but they also very frequently spent three or more days without eating or drinking; And it was not only men who practiced these austerities: women also imitated their example. There were communities of widows and virgins, who lived off the product of their wool yarns and fabrics, and were governed by the most respectable and holy communities for the formation and ordering of customs and, in addition, greater skill and culture for the instruction of intelligence. 71. In these communities no one was forced to austerities beyond their strength or what they refused to do; Nor did the others despise him for his weakness in enduring his life of penance and fasting. They were aware of the insistence with which charity is recommended in the sacred Scriptures, and they also knew that everything is pure for those who are pure, and that what enters the mouth is not defiled, but rather what comes out of it. They put all their effort into abstaining from some delicacies, not because of their filthiness, which they do not have, but to tame concupiscence and keep their charity towards one another immaculate and pure. 75. Do not gather in my presence those who profess to be Christians and ignore or do not show their strength and effectiveness with their works. Do not continue your invectives against that bunch of fools who, even within the true religion, are either superstitious or so completely given to sensual pleasures that they forget their promises to God. I know of many who are idolaters of tombs and paintings; of many who make excessive libations on the dead, and offer them banquets of excessive luxury, and bury themselves on top of the corpses, and even believe their orgies and drunkenness are religious acts; and, finally, I know of a large number who renounced the world only in words and consent to be oppressed by so many and such great requests of this century and they simply enjoy such burden and oppression. But why are you surprised to find, among so many people, those who, because of their bad lives, serve as an opportunity for you to seduce the simple and separate them from Catholic health, when within your very small sect you suffer death anguish if we demand the presentation of a single one of your chosen ones who faithfully fulfills those same precepts that your irrational superstition boasts about? In another volume I will show how vain, pernicious and sacrilegious your precepts are and how no one or almost no one of your sect puts them into practice. 76 I advise you to desist now from slander against the Catholic Church and from censuring the customs of those who she herself condemns and corrects with a mother's zeal as bad children. All those who are corrected by their good will and divine grace, recover through penitence what they lost through their sins. Those who, on the contrary, through their ill will add even more serious sins to their old sins, are tolerated, it is true, in the field of the Lord and are allowed to grow with the good seeds until the time comes to separate the tares from the good grain. Or if, because of the name of Christians they bear, they can be compared to chaff rather than thorns, it will not take long for the one who cleans the threshing floor to arrive, and then he will separate the chaff from the wheat and give each part what it deserves with utmost equity.

1. No one, I think, will doubt that the question of good and evil, which is what is dealt with here, is the object of morality. May the clarity and serenity of the vision of the intelligence of those who dedicate themselves to the investigation of these things be so great that they can contemplate from step to step that supreme good, nothing superior to it in excellence and sublimity, to which the pure and perfect rational soul submits! Because they would also see with what righteousness and justice it is called the supreme being, the first being, which is always the same, not at all identical with itself; which is inaccessible to all corruption or change; that is neither subject to time nor can it be any different today than it was yesterday. This being is what it truly is, since it means an essence subsistent in itself and inaccessible to any mutation. This being is God, who has no opposite, because being is only opposed by non-being? There is, therefore, no nature contrary to God. But since for the contemplation of these things we carry, on the contrary, the baggage of a wounded and dulled intelligence, either by childish opinions or by a perverse will, let us sacrifice everything possible to achieve some knowledge of such a lofty object, walking step by step, with caution, not as those who contemplate it usually seek, but as those who walk in darkness, groping.

7. I insist again for the third time on the nature of evil. The evil, you will answer, is corruption. Who can deny that this is evil in its generality? Isn't corruption against nature? Isn't she the one who damages? But my answer is that corruption is nothing in itself; It is not a substance, but exists in a substance that it affects. This substance that corruption touches is not corruption, it is not evil; because a thing that is attacked by corruption is deprived of its integrity and its purity; If it had no purity of which it could be deprived, it could not, evidently, be corrupted; and the purity that it possesses can only come from the source of all purity. Furthermore, what is corrupted is perverted; but perversion is deprivation of order, and order is a good, and, consequently, what attacks corruption is not devoid of good, and precisely the fact that it is not devoid of good makes possible its deprivation through corruption. From which it follows that if your kingdom of darkness is stripped, as you say, of all good, it cannot be subject to corruption, because it lacks everything that it can destroy.
