Quare ordinatio esse cogit, inordinatio vero non esse, quae perversio etiam nominatur atque corruptio. Quidquid igitur corrumpitur, eo tendit ut non sit. Iam vestrum est considere, quo cogat corruptio, ut possitis invenire summum malum: nam id est quo corruptio perducere nititur.

Ask what corruption is, you yourselves will see the answer just by looking at the change it makes in what is corruptible: it leaves its mark on everything it touches. Every object wounded by it decays from what it was and loses its permanence and even its being, because being and permanence are correlative: this is why the being that is immutable in the highest and supreme degree is immutable in itself. What changes to be better is because it tended towards perversion, towards loss? %of its essence, which must not be attributed in any way to the author of the essence. Some things change to be better, which is a tendency toward being: it is a return, a conversion, not a perversion or destruction; and because perversion is destruction of order, the tendency to being is a tendency to order; and once order is achieved, they touch the being itself insofar as the capacity of the creature suffers from it. Order reduces what it organizes to a certain unity. The essence of being is unity, and to the same extent that it is one it is being; The work of unity is to produce convenience and concord, by which composite things will have the measure of their being; while simple things are by themselves, since they are the unity; Those that are not imitate this unity by the harmony of their parts, and the measure of their union is the measure of their being. I conclude, therefore, that order produces being; Disorder, on the contrary, which can also be called perversion and corruption, produces non-being; and, consequently, everything that is corrupted tends, for this very reason, to no longer be. By what corruption produces you can discover the greatest evil, since this is the term to which corruption leads or leads.

27. But these blasphemies, which, coming from the heart, are always on your lips, prohibit you from continuing to proclaim your seal of the mouth to every wind, to seduce simple and ignorant people. Although it may be that you believe that its greatness and beauty consists solely in the abstention of meat and wine. In this case you need to know for what purpose you do it; For if the end to which we refer our actions, that is, in view of which we act, is not only without stain of sin, but also praiseworthy, our actions will follow the same fate and will be worthy of praise; But if, on the contrary, the end that we contemplate and look to when we do something is rightly and justly worthy of rebuke, there will be no one who will not disapprove and censure even the very thing we do. 28. It is said of Catiline that he could endure cold, hunger and thirst; This swine and sacrilegious man had this in common with our apostles. How is this parricide different from them, if not in the very different intentions he had? He suffered all this with the twisted goal of satisfying his most immoderate and inhuman passions, while the apostles had the very sane intention of dominating them and subjecting them to the rule of reason. You yourselves, when the great number of Catholic souls who are virgins are praised, have the perverse habit of saying: The mule is also a virgin. This foolish response, due to ignorance of Catholic doctrine, does not, however, mean the uselessness of continence if it does not refer for a determined reason to a very right end? Can't Catholics also make a comparison between your abstinence from wine and meats and! of donkeys, that of many birds and that of innumerable species of worms? But, in order not to fall into your folly, I will refrain from judging hastily until I examine with what intention you do it, since it is common among us to look only at the intention in this type of customs. If it is out of moderation and to curb your passions that you abstain from such foods and drinks, which delight and satisfy us, I listen to you with pleasure and I approve and praise you. But it's not like that.

29. The possible hypothesis can be made of the existence of a man so sparing and sober that, in order to control his appetite for eating and drinking, he only eats one meal a day; and at dinner, a few cooked vegetables seasoned with a crumb of bacon, two or three sips of wine to moisten the mouth, and so on daily. Let it now be done: - next to the previous hypothesis, another possible one, of another man to whom, without tasting wine or meat, is served at lunch all kinds of dishes, the most exquisite and pilgrim, and well sprinkled with all kinds of spices, and at dinner the same; and along with all this he savors varied and fine drinks, such as water sweetened with honey, cooked must, juices of various fruits, very similar to wine, but superior in softness and finesse, and without measure and without necessity, but for pure pleasure, and this not one day or two, but every day. Which of these two men, as far as food and drink are concerned, do you judge to have lived a more continent life? I do not believe you are so blind that you do not give preference to the one who eats and drinks little or soberly, over the spendthrift and glutton. 30. That is, at least, the song of truth, even if your error sings very differently. If the saint or chosen one who boasts of the three seals lived the life of the last one that I have just described, he might have the censure of one or two of the most serious and serious ones, but he could not be condemned as a violator of the seal. If, on the other hand, this same saint or chosen one comes to dine just once with the man of the first hypothesis, and smears his lips a little with a crumb of bacon or eats a small piece of ham, and refreshes his mouth with a sip of distorted wine, by the authority of your founder, not without admiration, but at the same time with your consent, he will be judged as a violator of the seal and, as such, condemned to hell. Oh! I ask you with the greatest interest: abandon your error, listen to reason, resist habit or custom a little. Can you think of anything more crazy and perverse?

Is it possible to say or think more foolishly than to a man whose belly is so full of mushrooms, rice, truffles, cakes, pepper and other spices; who glories in belching all this, and so every day, is not judged a violator of the three seals, that is, of the rule of holiness, while the same one who eats only poorly seasoned legumes and in quantities barely sufficient for the needs of his body, and does not drink more than three sips of corrupted wine for the sake of health, for just once he passes from those banquets to this most frugal meal, Are certain punishments prepared for him?

31. But the Apostle says: It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine. As if any of us would deny the goodness of this advice! What must be kept in mind are the reasons that I already mentioned and are expressed in these words: Do not beware of the lusts of the flesh, or those that the apostle Saint Paul himself later indicates, such as, for example, restraining gluttony, which tends to become more rabid and immoderate with these things; Do not scandalize your brothers or prevent the weak from doing acts of idolatry. At the time the Apostle was writing this, a lot of meat was sold in the market, offered to idols, and libations were made to the false gods of the Gentiles; And that is why many brothers who were not yet strong and well instructed in the faith, who had an obligation to go to the market, preferred to abstain from meat and wine rather than fall, without knowing it, into what they believed to be a communication with idols. Others, more educated and stronger in faith, despised these beliefs with more certainty, because they knew that food could not defile except through a bad conscience, as the word of the Lord says: What enters through the mouth does not defile the soul, but what comes out of it. However, they kept in mind the weakness of the brothers, which led them to abstain from these things, so as not to cause them to be scandalized. This is not a simple conjecture, it is a fact recorded in the very epistles of Saint Paul. When you plead these words: It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine, why do you not complete the Apostle's thought with what follows: nor do anything that could offend, or scandalize, or weaken your brother? 53. These principles lead you to prohibit giving bread to the poor, and yet mercy, or rather, envy, will inspire you to give him money. This poor sinner covers with dirt and impurities the portion of God who longs to resume flight towards his kingdom; And the most serious thing is that you cooperate with this crime with your money, and yet, your prudence, as great as it is, comes to see the difference between putting the victim in the hands of the murderer and putting the money to buy it and sacrifice it. Because one of two things will happen: either the death of the beggar, if he does not acquire bread to eat, or the death of the bread, if he acquires it; The first is a real homicide, the same as the second, according to your doctrine, and you are responsible for both. Now I remember that gradation that frequently worried me when I heard your explanations. If smallness authorizes the destruction of a flea, nothing will prevent taking the life of a fly, which has its birth in a bean. If you do not spare the fly, why not kill the somewhat stronger insect whose offspring is surely smaller than the fly? It will also follow that there will be no obstacle to destroying a little bird whose offspring is of the same size as this fly, and the locust and the mouse are the same as their offspring. I will not go on any further, because it is enough to see that one step at a time will reach the elephant, until one can kill without any sin this monstrous beast, which, due to its smallness, can without sin destroy a flea. 66. But when you so vehemently oppose the union of the sexes, which chains the soul to the flesh, and with even greater vehemence and energy you affirm that through the food of the saints the soul comes out of the slavery of the seeds, do you not at the same time confirm, oh wretches, the suspicions that are formed against you? Why, when you eat wheat, beans and lentils and other seeds, is it believed that it is your will to give freedom to the soul and the same should not be believed with respect to the seeds of animals? What you say about the impurity of the flesh of a dead animal, because it has no soul, you cannot say about the seed of a living animal, which, according to you, has a soul chained that will manifest itself in the offspring, and in which you confess the soul of the Manichaean himself is buried. And since such seeds cannot be presented to you by your listeners to purify them, who will not fall into the suspicion that you yourselves carry out these secret purifications and that you hide these infamous actions from them, for fear that they will abandon you? And if you do not do them, and God wants it to be so, do you not see to what suspicions your superstition gives free rein and how irrational it is to be irritated against those who judge in this way, giving them reasons, since you proclaim that by food and drink you free the souls from the bodies and the senses? 67. Now it is quite clear what judgment your doctrine of the three seals deserves. Such are your works, such is the purpose of your admirable precepts, where nothing is certain, nor true, nor rational, nor harmless, but everything on the contrary, doubtful; Furthermore, everything is, without a doubt, extremely false, contradictory, absurd and abominable. In short, so many and such serious sins are discovered in your customs that, if someone of any capacity wanted to file a case against all of them, for each one there would be only a few pages of a volume. If you observed such precepts and practiced such teachings, you would be the most inept, foolish and ignorant person in the world; But, since you are only content with praise and with teaching what you do not practice, it follows that it is not possible to imagine or meet people who are neither more false, nor more dangerous, nor with worse intentions than you.,68. During the entire nine years that I listened to the explanations of your doctrine with great vigilance and assiduity, I could not meet a single one of your elect who, from the point of view of your precepts, had not been caught in sins or had not given rise to suspicion. We heard that many were given to wine and meat and the pleasures of bathing; and others were accused, without the possibility of reply, of corrupting their neighbors' wives. Such is the opinion that you have formed of Adam and Eve: it is a very long fable; Here I will only touch on what is related to my issue. INTRODUCTION

In the life of Saint Augustine, friendship is one of the springs that moved the tireless activity of that spirit, always eager for the infinite, and who, despite being overwhelmed by unavoidable occupations, which weighed on his shoulders as defender and oracle of the Church and zealous pastor, and not having hardly a moment of free time, always, however, always found a way, at the cost of how many sacrifices 1 we do not know, to satisfy the wishes of his friends^ who wanted have each of them some radgaiaa of his inexhaustible wealth. Everyone asked him to solve their doubts, to give them weapons with which to respond adequately to the innumerable heretics that swarmed everywhere in the 5th century; and he, condescending to everyone, was distributing the treasures of his most brilliant intelligence and most ardent heart. Totally devoted to the defense of the Church, he was the servant of all, and Christians throughout the Empire believed they had the right to address their queries to him; He denied no one the consolation of his answers, even if they were questions he had already resolved in one of his other treatises. And selecting from his works what he thought most appropriate, correcting himself in some places, ratifying and providing new reasons in others, he took upon himself such a heavy burden that today we cannot explain how a bishop, with the multiple occupations that this position entailed, was able to complete such a large number of works, some of which were of such magnitude that they alone could very well fill the entire life of a man. And when, due to his many occupations, he was forced to postpone the execution of what was requested of him, he alleged the reasons that impelled him to do so, not wanting to appear careless or negligent when it came to doing a favor. Many examples of this can be seen in his letters and other treatises. But, because it is treated

from a brother of Lorenzo—to whom the Enchiridion is dedicated—, I will choose the introduction to the treatise entitled De octo Dulcitti quaestionibus, *n which says: "At Easter I received your art, which you sent me from Carthage. After those holy days I found myself forced to set out for that same city, and there the multitude of my occupations, great in excess, did not allow me to dictate anything in the three months that I spent there. I remained. The first fifteen days following my departure I had to dedicate to clearing up the affairs that had accumulated during my absence; and as soon as possible, I began the work you entrusted to me, since there is nothing more pleasant for me." This little book, composed of fragments of his other works—from this one he copied chapters 67-69, 109 and 110—was addressed to Dulcicio, brother of this Lorenzo to whom he dedicates this treatise; This is how the words "item in eo libro cui titulus est De fide, spe et caritate, quem scripsi ad filium meum fratrem tuum Laurentium" are usually interpreted 2. As for the recipient of the Enchiridion, we are completely unaware of the relationships that united him with Saint Augustine. The book does not make any personal reference, other than the "dilectissime filii Laurenti" in the first chapter and "teque in eius membris plurimum diligens" in the last, which are not enough to satisfy our curiosity. It certainly seems to be a person of great culture, from the praise that the author pays him in the first chapter, as well as from some of the questions he addresses to Saint Augustine, such as this one: "How far can reason go in defense of religion, and in what matters, which surpass reason, must we be guided only by faith", a question that a person of little culture would not have asked. His name is Lorenzo, as it appears in all the manuscripts; some of them give him the title of "Primicerio" or director of the choir of the Roman Church, while others call him "chief of the notaries" of the same city. Lorenzo, by letter, proposed to Saint Augustine the development of certain themes in an easily manageable book. The questions were the following: truths to be believed and errors to be avoided, scope of reason in matters of religion, principle and crowning of the Christian life, true and proper foundation of the Catholic faith.
As the subject is very varied, we believe that it will be convenient to give a brief summary of the content of the book, and its great importance will soon become clear, since

We can say that it is an authentic compendium of almost all the doctrines of the Saint. To the questions proposed by Lorenzo, Saint Augustine answers that the worship of God is the true wisdom of man; that God must be worshiped by faith, hope and charity; and since these three virtues are contained in the Sunday Prayer and in the Symbol, it will be enough to expose them to fully answer the questions posed. In chapter 8 he tells us summarily what each of these three virtues consists of. Next he explains the content of the Symbol, part of which constitutes almost the entire book (ce. 9-113). In this part, rich in ideas and precise in exposition, he explains the main dogmas of Christianity, intermingling some moral questions, since these two sciences—moral and dogmatic—are very closely united in this treatise, a general thing in the treatises of the Saint. We see, for example, that he talks about lying, considering it intrinsically bad, unlike error, which can sometimes even be useful to us and is not always a sin. He expressly defends that not even saints can go through this life without some sin; well understood that these are venial sins. It greatly highlights the seriousness of sins. Penance is necessary to achieve the remission of sins, also exposing the doctrine about works of mercy. But although a part of this treatise is dedicated to these moral questions, the dogmatic doctrine largely predominates, carefully exposing those truths that were most fought by the heretics of his time, whom, without naming them once in the course of the work, he does not lose sight of.

When speaking of evil he fights the Manichaeans, but the ones his attacks are almost always directed primarily at are the Pelagians, defending with great diligence almost all the truths attacked by them: the "initium fidei" and penance are gifts from God, he admits with them that one cannot believe, hope and love if J.O's will concurs, but it must be prepared by the Lord; All of man's evils come from original sin, whose immediate consequences—concupiscence and ignorance—mean that we not only need grace to know what to do, but also medicine to cure our illness and defeat this carnal concupiscence; that original sin is transmitted to all men, making them subject to eternal damnation; hence children also have a need for baptism. He goes on to deal with grace, affirming its gratuitousness and necessity so that one can deserve something in the supernatural order; and, finabnen-

te, speaks of the mercy of God towards his chosen ones, who, forming with the wicked a single mass of perdition, since Adam's sin made all men guilty of the just judgment of God, he very kindly chose them to show in them his infinite goodness. To each erroneous statement or denial of these heretics Saint Augustine opposes the eternal truths of the Church, never better defended and loved. He speaks at length about the divine and human nature of Christ and the union of both natures in forming the one person of the Savior, with such precision that many of his formulas have been passed down to the theologians of posterity; Also the "Quicumque" symbol has adopted some. He condemned in advance several heresies, such as Nestorianism. adoptionism and monophysitism, it being an extremely strange thing that he has been accused of this error; It is enough to read chapters 33 to 41 carefully to be convinced of his doctrine. Although he did not write any special treatise on this matter, except letter 137, to Volusianus, in all his great works he clarified it with vivid brilliance, being the center of his theology and his religious life; for, as it says in this same treatise, "certum propriumque fidei fundamentum, Chuistus est" (c. 5); Christ is also the center of the history of humanity, as can be seen in chapter 118. "Saint Augustine," says Father Cayré, "has strongly emphasized the role of Christ the mediator. God became man to cure the heart of man of pride, but, above all, to reconcile him with God. He fulfilled the first mission by his humility. No Father has insisted as much as Saint Augustine on this moral side of the incarnation, on this "humility of God" (c. 108); it is a divine person, it is the Word who has humbled himself. He fulfills the second by his death, which has been a true atoning sacrifice offered by Christ to his Father, by virtue of a substitution... This redemption is universal; it extends to all sins and all sinners, but not to the fallen angels; the elect will fill the voids left by them in heaven. To return to grace those who have committed serious sins after baptism, the Church has received from its divine founder the power to forgive all kinds of sins, through penance, and, although it does not call it a sacrament, it nevertheless exposes its way of feeling with sufficient clarity.
We have already indicated the distinction he makes between serious sins ("peccata gravia, crimina"), which separate them from the kingdom of God, and light ones ("levia, minutissima, quotidia").

These three kinds of sins are forgiven by three different types of penance: by baptism the original sin and all the personal sins that have been committed are erased: "quod (munus baptismatis) contra origínale peccatum donatum est...; et tamen activa quoque peeeata^quaecumque corde, ore, opere commissa invenerit, tollit" "(c. 64); But since while living in this mortal body, no matter how much one has advanced in virtue, it is impossible to live without sin, two other kinds of penance have been granted to us to obtain its forgiveness. By the first, all venial sins are erased, and it consists of prayer—especially in the Sunday Prayer—together with the works of mercy, and in a particular way in the forgiveness of enemies, which is the most excellent almsgiving: "de quotidianis autem brevibus levibusque peccatis... quotidiana fidelium oratio satisfiit." Through the second, forgiveness of all sins, no matter how enormous they may be, is obtained from the Church: "'sed ñeque de ipsis criminibus- quamlibet magnis remittendis in sancta Ecclesia, Dei misericordia desperanda est agentibus paenitentiam secundum modum sui cuiusque peceati" (c. 65). Can anyone expect what they do not believe? However, you can believe something that you do not expect. For what faithful person does not believe in the punishments of the wicked? And yet, does not expect them, and whoever believes that they are hovering over him and tries to avoid them by a spontaneous movement of the soul, is rather said to fear them than to expect them. Trying to distinguish these two things, a poet wrote: "Let it be lawful to wait for him who fears." Another poet, although more elegant, said with less propriety: "If I could have expected such great pain." And some grammarians also use this example to indicate the inappropriateness of the language, claiming that he wrote "hope" instead of "fear." There is, therefore, faith in good and bad things, since good and bad things are believed in the same way, and this with good faith, not bad. There is also faith about things past, present and future; and so we believe that Christ died—that he belongs to the past—, we believe that he is seated at the right hand of the Father—that he is present—and we believe that he will come to judge—a future thing. Likewise there is faith about one's own things and those of others. In fact, we all believe that we have begun to exist at some point, and that we have not always existed, and the same with other men, and so we believe many other things; In the same way, we not only believe many things about men that refer to religion, but also about angels. Hope is only about good and future things and they refer to the one who is said to have hope for them. This being so, in the same way that faith and hope are distinguished by their term, so also, for these causes, a rational distinction must mediate between them. Faith and hope agree that both the object of one and the other is invisible. NO EVIL WOULD EXIST WITHOUT THE GOOD

Without good, evil could not exist. The good that lacks all evil is the absolute good; On the contrary, the one to which evil is attached is a corrupt or corruptible good; and where good does not exist, no evil is possible. From this a strange conclusion is deduced: that, since every substance, as such, is a good, it seems that, when the corrupted substance is called bad, it is affirmed that evil is the same as good, and that evil does not exist except in so far as good exists; for all nature is a good, and there would be no bad thing if that same thing that is bad were not a substance. From which it follows that evil does not occur without good. And although this may seem absurd, however, the connection of this reasoning necessarily requires this conclusion. We must avoid that prophetic sentence from falling on us: Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who make darkness out of light and light out of darkness, and turn bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter! And yet the Lord says: An evil man brings out evil things from his evil treasure. And, since man is a substance, what else is the "bad man" but bad nature? Finally, if man is some good, since he is a substance, what is an evil man but an evil good? Distinguishing, however, these two things, we see that he is not evil because he is a man, nor good because he is perverse, but good because he is a man, and bad because he is perverse. GOOD AND EVIL, EVEN THOUGH THEY ARE CONTRARY THINGS, CAN EXIST AT THE SAME TIME IN THE SAME THING. EVIL COMES FROM GOOD

According to what has been explained so far, that rule of the dialecticians is not fulfilled: Contrary qualities cannot occur in the same thing and at the same time; because we see that good and evil coexist. The air cannot be both dark and transparent; no food or drink is both sweet and bitter; In the same way, a body cannot be black and white at the same time and in the same place, nor beautiful where it is deformed; The same thing happens in many, if not all contrary things. Everyone admits that good and evil are contrary, and yet both can exist simultaneously in the same being; Furthermore, evil cannot exist in any way without and outside of good, although good can exist without evil. The man or the angel may not be unjust, but injustice cannot exist except in the man or the angel; and man and angel are good as such, but bad as unjust. These two contrary things go together in such a way that in no way could any evil exist without good, a! which may be attached; For not only would corruption not find where to take root, but not even where to come from, if there were not something that is subject to corruption; and if it were not good, it could not be corrupted, since corruption is nothing other than the expulsion of good. Consequently, evils have had their origin in goods, and if it is not in some good, they do not exist, since the nature of evil would have no place to originate from. If it existed, as a nature, it would necessarily be good: incorruptible, a great good, or corruptible, a lesser good, which, by discrediting corruption, could harm it.

On some occasions we deceive ourselves with serious damage, on others with minor damage, on others with very slight damage and sometimes even with some benefit. We deceive ourselves to serious harm when we do not believe what leads us to eternal life, or, on the contrary, we believe what leads us down the path of perdition. He is deceived with less harm if, approving what is false as true, some temporary misfortunes befall him, which, however, Christian resignation converts into its own benefit; This is what happens when someone, considering a bad man to be a good man, takes advantage of his good reputation to cause him some harm; But he who judges good the evil and receives no evil from him, is not deceived nor does that prophetic curse fall on him: Woe to those who call evil good! MAN'S REPARATION IS NOT DUE TO HIS MERITS OR FREE WILL, BUT TO GRACE

Can this portion of the human race to whom God promised liberation and the eternal kingdom be reborn by the merits of their own works? No way. For what good can one who is lost accomplish, unless he is freed from perdition? Perhaps by the free will of his will? This is not possible either, since, by misusing free will, man lost himself and his free will. For in the same way that someone who commits suicide kills himself while he is still alive, and by taking his life he ceases to exist, and after death he cannot give himself life, so also, sinning through free will, he lost it through the triumph of sin, since each person is a slave to the one who triumphed over him. This sentence is from the apostle Peter, and, being true, I ask: what freedom can a slave from sin have, except when it delights him to sin? For only he who willingly executes the will of his master serves as a degree, and, according to this, he who is a slave to sin is free to sin. From which it follows that he will not be free to act justly, unless, freed from sin, he begins to be a servant of justice. True freedom consists in the joy of doing well, and is also pious servitude through obedience to the law. But where will this freedom come to man, alienated and sold, except by the ransom of him who said: If the Son will free you, you will be truly free? And before this begins to take place in man, who can boast of free will in any good work, if he is not yet free to do good, unless he becomes proud, puffed up by pride? And the Apostle represses it when he says: By grace you have been saved through faith.

Is the will itself, as it is written, prepared by God? On the contrary, if it has been said: It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God, who has mercy, because this depends on both, namely, of the will of man and of divine mercy, in such a way that we understand this saying: It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God, who has mercy, as if it were said that the will of man alone is not enough, if it is not accompanied by the mercy of God; Therefore, God's mercy would not be sufficient if it were not accompanied by the will of man. And if, because the human will alone is not sufficient, it was rightly said: Not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God, who has mercy, to indicate that the will of man alone is not sufficient, why, on the contrary, was it not rightly said not of God, who has compassion, but of the man who wills, since it is not the exclusive work of God's mercy either? Finally, if no Christian would dare to say: not of God, who has compassion, but of the man who wants, so as not to openly contradict the Apostle, it only remains to correctly understand the sentence: It is not of the one who wants nor of the one who runs, but of God, who has mercy, in such a way that everything is attributed to God, who prepares the good will by helping it and helps it once prepared. The good will of man precedes many of God's gifts, but not all; and among those whom she does not precede is herself. Both things are read in the sacred Scriptures: He will prevent me with his mercy; and: His mercy accompanies me. He warns those who do not want so that they will; and whoever wants, he accompanies so that he does not want in vain. For why are we commanded to pray for our enemies, who truly do not want to live piously, but so that God may work in them to desire Himself? And in the same way, why are we commanded to ask so that we may receive, but so that he who has caused us to ask may do what we ask? Then we pray for our enemies that the mercy of God may precede them, as it preceded us also; and we pray for us that his mercy may accompany us.

THE BIRTH OF CHRIST, BECAUSE IT IS THE WORK OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, MAKES GRACE MANIFEST

The same only begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, our only Lord, was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. The Holy Spirit is a gift from God and a gift equal to the one who gives it; and for this reason, God is also the Holy Spirit and not less than the Father and the Son. Therefore, what else indicates the intervention of the Holy Spirit in the birth of Jesus Christ, if not grace? For the Virgin having asked the angel how what he announced to her would happen, since she would not know a man, the angel answered her: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the virtue of the Most High will cover you with its shadow, and for this reason the son begotten by you will be holy, he will be called the Son of God. Saint Joseph received the same response when he tried to repudiate the woman he saw pregnant as an adulteress, having respected her, with these words: Do not be afraid to receive Mary, your wife, into your home, since what was conceived in her is the work of the Holy Spirit; that is, what you suspect to be from another man is the work of the Holy Spirit.

JUDGING THE LIVING AND THE DEAD CAN BE UNDERSTOOD IN TWO WAYS

In two ways it can be understood that Christ will judge the living and the dead. We can understand by living those whom upon his coming he will find here, not yet dead, but living in this body; and for dead, those who have ceased or will cease to exist before the judgment comes. We can also understand the living as the just, and the dead as the sinners, since the just must also be Judged. The judgment of God can sometimes be counted among unpleasant things, as when it is said: but those who have done evil will come out of their graves, for the resurrection of judgment; others, among the good or pleasant, as it is written: Save me, O God, for the honor of your name, and judge me in your power. By the judgment of God, in effect, the separation is made between the good and the bad, so that those who are to be freed from evil, those who are not to perish with the perverse, the good, may be separated to the right. That is why the Psalmist exclaims: Judge me, O God!; and as if explaining what he has said, he adds: and separate me from this impious mob.

Therefore, everything that is done out of useful mercy refers to what the Lord says: Give alms, and everything will be pure for you. TO WHAT EXTENT AND WHO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THE SACRIFICE OF THE ALTAR AND THE ALMS THAT ARE MADE FOR THE DEAD-

It cannot be denied that the souls of the deceased are relieved by the piety of their living relatives, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or when alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, when they lived, deserved to be able to benefit them later. For there is a certain way of living, neither so good that you do not miss these things after death, nor so bad that they do not benefit you; But there is such a degree in good that he who possesses it does not miss them, and, on the contrary, there is such a degree in evil that he cannot be helped with them when he passes from this life. Therefore, here man acquires all the merit with which he can be relieved or oppressed after death. No one expects to deserve before God, when he has died, what he despised during life. These things, which the Church so frequently practices to help its dead, are not opposed to that apostolic sentence in which it is said: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the payment due for the good or bad actions he has done while he has been clothed with his body. Because each one also, while living in his body, earned the merit that these things could benefit him. But they are not useful to everyone, and why are they not useful to everyone, if not because of the diversity of life that each one had while he lived? Thus, the sacrifices, whether that of the altar, or any kind of alms, that are offered for all the baptized deceased, for the very good, are thanksgiving; for the not very badvticnen In order to appease divine justice; For the very bad, although they are of no benefit to the deceased, they are of some consolation to the living... The Sunday Prayer, according to the formula of Saint Matthew, seems to contain seven petitions: in the first three, eternal goods are requested; in the remaining four, the temporary ones that are necessary to achieve the eternal ones. Because all that we ask in these first three petitions: Hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, both on earth and in heaven (which some, not unintentionally, have understood in the body and in the spirit), all these things must be preserved, without a doubt, for all eternity; which, begun here, continue to develop in us as we advance in the good; but once they are perfectly achieved, which we must hope to achieve in the other life, they will always be possessed. IN SAN LUCAS ONLY FIVE PETITIONS ARE CONTAINED; IT IS AGREED WITH SAN MATEO

But the evangelist Saint Luke in the Sunday Prayer expressed not seven petitions, but five; but it certainly does not disagree with the former, but rather with its very brevity it warns us how those seven are to be understood. For the name of God is sanctified in the spirit, and his kingdom will come in the resurrection of the body. And so, Saint Luke wanting to indicate that the third request is, in a certain way, a repetition of the previous two, omitting it makes it understood more clearly. Then he adds three others, that of the daily bread, that of the forgiveness of sins and that of the flight from temptation. But the one that he put last: But deliver us from evil, he also omitted, so that we would understand that it should refer to the previous one, which speaks of temptation. That is why he said: But deliver us from evil, and not "and deliver us," as indicating that all this was a single request (as it is a single statement to say do not want this, but that), so that everyone may know that they are delivered from evil in that they are not put into temptation.

CHAPTER CXXI CHARITY IS THE END OF ALL PRECEPTS

32. All the divine precepts are directed to charity, of which the Apostle says: The end of the precept is charity, which is born from a pure heart, from a good conscience and from a sincere faith. Therefore, the end of every precept is charity, that is, every precept refers to charity. But that which, out of fear of punishment or for some carnal intention, is done in a way that does not refer to that charity that the Holy Spirit pours into our hearts, is still not fulfilled as it should be, no matter how much it seems to be done. This charity is the love of God and neighbor, and in truth all the Law and the Prophets are contained in these two precepts; and the Gospel and the Apostles can also be added, since this sentence comes from no other place: The end of the precept is charity, and this other: God is charity. Therefore, everything that God prescribes, such as, for example, you shall not fornicate; and that which does not command, but recommends only as healthy advice, such as: it is good for a man not to touch a woman, then they are fulfilled correctly when they refer to love.

INTRODUCTION

Perhaps today the issue that stirred African Christianity with such feverish activity for a long century would seem a bit trivial to us: the Donatist heresy. The moral ideological environment has been evolving over the centuries even within the Church, without, of course, affecting its dogma in any substantial way. The issues that seem trivial to us today were of utmost importance in past centuries in the order of ideas and customs. What seems clear to us today and beyond any doubt cost our ancestors great sweat. Sticking to our topic, the presentation of the Donatist conflict, the doctrinal points are so studied and their consequences so clear, that it would seem absurd to any moderately educated Christian to think about the dignity or unworthiness of the minister in order to remain calm when he receives the sacraments. Perhaps this is an indication of a decrease in their esteem; but even with this inconvenience we see how much progress has been made in the correct formation of conscience. On the other hand, in the primitive Church, which so closely felt the influence of the footprints of Christ and the perfume of the blood of the martyrs, the delicacy of conscience and loving respect for divine things floated in the atmosphere. And, consequently, the faults that could disfigure the immaculate purity of those most sacred dogmas were the object of the most indignant abomination and the most fiery reproach. Therefore, taking these very just sentiments to the extreme, it is not strange that we see errors or heresies abound from the first moments around the readmission of sinners into the bosom of the Church. Such was the inspiration of mountainism, whose leader and founder, Montano, gives name to the sect that claimed to be like the quintessence of Christianity and has as its principle an exaggerated rigorism, from which even more exaggerated consequences are derived, such as the unforgivability of sins committed.

Until then he had only written a few occasional letters, and rather particular ones, and sporadic objections when dealing with other matters, in addition, of course, to the exhortations of his sermons and his talks. Was it because he did not give the issue the importance it had, or because the situation did not seem so serious, or because he hoped that little by little, without the need for serious concerns, such an unstable building would collapse by itself? Perhaps also contributing to this was his commitment to the fight against Manichaeism, which, because it was more dangerous and had seduced him in his youth, deserved a more urgent remedy. Since the year 400, systematic treaties against the Donatists have come to light: sometimes motivated by the writings of one of their hierarchs, and other times, expressly dealing with some capital point of their heresy. To the first group belong: Contra epistolam Romaniani libri tres, Contra Htteras Petüiani libri tres, Contra Cresconium grammaticum donatistam libri quattuor, De sole baptismo contra Petilianum, Contra Gaudentium (libri duo). Among the treatises that are not in epistolary form, the following stand out: De baptismo contra donatistas (libri septem), Breviculus collationis cum donatistis, Ad donatistas post cottationem. Its title itself tells us what it is about. An intermediate place between these two classes of anti-Donatist writings occupies the book De unitate Ecclesiae, which the B. A. C. has chosen as representative of the entire contest. And not without reason, since it not only gives us an overall impression of the terms he arrived at, but is perhaps the masterpiece of Saint Augustine against the Donatists, either as an index or summary of his errors, or as a complete and finished pulverization of his arguments. • ^Following the Saint's explanation of the points of disagreement; the quotation and commentary, perhaps somewhat heavy, but forceful, of the passages of sacred Scripture; the sagacity with which he goes out to meet the subterfuges used by his adversaries; the concessions that, in his desire to convince and attract them, he manages to make them; the highness of vision and the fiery charity that flow through his reasoning, one cannot help but surrender to that dialectic so characteristic of him and find himself in the dilemma of accepting without reservation his conclusions or renouncing the use of that faculty that we call discursive, and whose main tendency is the diligent search for the truth.

is clearly stated in the summary or argument. As the basis of the entire Donatist dispute, the question is clarified as to whether the Church, founded by Christ and fertilized with his blood, has substantially degenerated due to the indignities of some of its members and has disappeared from the face of the earth, leaving the Donatist faction as the only stronghold. The problem is really no other: as in any discussion, once the principles have been established, the only thing to do is to abide by its consequences. All other accusations about the surrender of the sacred books, about persecution, about rebaptism, etc., are corollaries of that basic truth. Once the true Church has been demonstrated and admitted, it is the Church that has to judge those other secondary issues, which, on the other hand, being the work of some of its members, can never stain the Church or change or distort its nature. That is why we say that this is the fundamental work of Saint Augustine against the Donatists, because it is directed at the key point of all differences. The other discrepancies have been addressed particularly in various works; and although circumstantially, in the course of his fruitful literary and homiletic activity, all those discrepancies come up and the true and only Church is warmly referred to and defended, in the De unitate Ecclesiae is where the Saint squeezes to its intimate core the testimonies of Scripture in favor of it, demonstrating even the most obvious evidence the weakness of the arguments with which the Donatists try to shield themselves from their errors. So that there is no other recourse than to sing the psalm to which we previously alluded, composed for the illustration of the people, and in which, as severely as they rhythmically, the alternatives of discord, testimonies of Scripture, truths of the Catholic creed, parade: Omnes qui gaudetis de pace moda veruin iudicate.

INTRODUCTION

Some writers denied Augustinian paternity to this pamphlet, which today no one doubts. The holy Doctor himself recognizes it in his letter 231, addressed to Count Dario. It is probably a sermon preached to the people after the year 399. Saint Augustine sets out to refute what he calls "remnants of infidelity", demonstrating the need to believe. Faith is indispensable in the ordinary course of life. Without it, neither friendship, nor family love, nor social relationships can exist. It is necessary, therefore, to believe many things without seeing them. We believe in Christ, whom we did not see; but our faith does not lack sufficient reasons to believe. Prophecies faithfully fulfilled: here is the great test of our faith. The Church is the fact visible to all among the nations. She, with a maternal voice, invites us to contemplate her, to come to her loving bosom. Saint Augustine sees in her the queen seated at the right of the heavenly Bridegroom, dressed in gold, respected and loved, fruitful in works of holiness, blessed by all peoples. The Church that we now see, which was previously promised, and precisely in the same sacred Scriptures, which announce other Christian truths, is an index of the past and a preview and announcement of the future. The Jews preserve the sacred books where the prophecies are written. They were not exterminated, so that they would carry everywhere the documents that prove our Christian faith. Even if the prophecies concerning Christ and his Church did not exist, the admirable conversion of the world to faith in a crucified man would be reason enough to believe This is a miracle, and a stupendous miracle. A crucified man would have been able to do nothing if he were not an incarnate God. The faithful must be vigilant so that they are not seduced by pagans, heretics, or bad Christians,

and remain separated from them with the heart until reaching eternal life. Saint Augustine uses in defense of the faith the great arguments that the apologists of Christianity would later use: miracles, prophecies, the wonderful spread of the Christian faith, the testimony of the martyrs, the existence of the Church of Christ as a visible fact. The luminous and anointed word of pastoral zeal of the great Bishop of Hippo today ignites in souls that divine light and that sacred fire that centuries ago illuminated and consumed the multitudes of Africa and the entire world.

In the first place, we must warn those fools, so slaves of the eyes of the body that they persuade themselves that they should not believe what they do not see, that they themselves believe and know many things that cannot be perceived with those senses. You present it outside so that we can see it with our bodily eyes, nor is it inside our soul so that we can see it with our understanding. They say these things as if someone were told to believe what is already before their eyes. It is necessary to believe some temporary things that we do not see, so that we are worthy of seeing the eternal things that we believe. And you, who do not want to believe more than what you see, listen for a moment: you see the objects present with the eyes of the body; you see your thoughts and affections with the eyes of the soul. Now tell me, please: how do you see your friend's affection? Because affection cannot be seen with bodily eyes. Do you see, perchance, with the eyes of the soul what happens in the soul of another? And, if you don't see it, how will you reciprocate friendly feelings, when you don't believe what you can't see? Will you reply, perhaps, that you see the friend's affection in his works? You will see, in fact, the works of your friend, you will hear his words; but you will have to believe in its affection, because it cannot be seen or heard, since it is not a color or a figure that enters through the eyes, nor a sound or a song that penetrates through the ears, nor an internal affection that manifests itself to consciousness. It only remains for you to believe what you cannot see, nor hear, nor know through the testimony of conscience, so that you are not isolated in life without the consolation of friendship, or the affection of your friend is left without fair correspondence. Where is your purpose of not believing more than what you see externally with the eyes of the body or internally with the eyes of the soul? You see that your affection moves you to believe in affection that is not yours; and where neither your sight nor your understanding can reach, your faith reaches. With the eyes of the body you see the face of your friend, and with the eyes of the soul you see your own fidelity; But you cannot love the fidelity of a friend if you do not also have the faith that inclines you to believe what you do not see in him; although man can deceive by lying love and hiding his evil intention. And, if he does not intend to do harm, he feigns charity, which he does not have, to obtain some benefit from you. 3. But you say that, if you believe your friend, although you cannot see his heart, it is because you tested him in your misfortune and knew his faithfulness when he did not abandon you in moments of danger. Do you imagine, by chance, that we have to long for our misfortune to taste the love of friends?

No one could taste the sweetness of friendship if they did not first taste the bitterness of adversity; nor would he enjoy the pleasure of true love who did not suffer the torment of anguish and pain. Why should the happiness of having good friends not be feared rather than desired, if it cannot be achieved without one's own misfortune? And yet it is very true that even in prosperity one can have a good friend, although their love is more easily tested in adversity.

8. But just as by the evidence that is seen we believe in friendly feelings without being seen, in the same way, the Church, which we now see, is an index of the past and a foretaste and announcement of the future, which is not seen, but is shown in the same Scriptures, in which it is announced. At the moment of the prediction, nothing was visible: neither the past, which can no longer be seen, nor the present, which not everything is visible. When these things began to take place, from those already past to those present, all the prophecies relating to Christ and his Church have been fulfilled in an ordered series. To this series belong: the final judgment, the resurrection of the dead, the eternal damnation of the evil with the devil and the eternal glory of the good with Christ. All these things were also announced and must be fulfilled. Why should we not believe the past and future things that we do not see, having the proof of both in the present things that we see, and reading or hearing read in the prophetic books that the past, the present and the future were all announced before they happened? 9. If you have this suspicion, carefully examine the books of the Jews, our enemies. Read there all these things of which we have spoken, announced of Christ, in whom we believe, and of his Church, which we see from the first works in the propagation of the faith, to the eternal blessedness of the kingdom of heaven. When you read, do not be surprised that the owners of those books, blinded by hatred, do not understand these things. For this lack of intelligence was already announced by the prophets, and had to be fulfilled, like all other prophecies, so that the Jews, for secret reasons of divine justice, would receive the punishment they deserved for their sins. The one they crucified, and to whom they gave gall and vinegar, although he was hanging on the tree, for the love of those whom he was to bring out of darkness to light, said to the Father: Forgive them, because they do not know what they do, however, because of the others whom, by secret divine judgments, he was to abandon, announced long before by the mouth of the prophet: They put gall in my food, and when I was thirsty, they gave me vinegar to drink; Let their table be a snare and their prosperity a stumbling block; Let the light of their eyes be extinguished so that they do not see, and their loins are always wavering. With eyes without light they go everywhere, carrying with them the luminous proofs of our cause, so that with them it is proven and they are reproved. This Jewish people was not exterminated, but dispersed throughout the world, so that, carrying with them the prophecies of the grace that they received, they would serve us everywhere to more easily convince the unbelievers. The same thing that I am saying has been announced by the prophet: Do not kill them, lest they forget your law; scatter them with your strength. They were not killed because they did not forget what they had read or heard read in the sacred Scriptures. If, although they did not understand those holy books, they had completely forgotten them, they would have perished with the Jewish rites. Because if the Jews did not know the Law and the Prophets, they would not serve us at all. That is why they were not killed, but dispersed: so that their memories may be useful to us, even if they do not have the faith that saves. In their hearts they are our adversaries, and in their Scriptures our servants and witnesses.

But the faith that the Church demands of those who approach and gather into its bosom is not irrational either. Saint Augustine says it exhaustively in this work of his. De utüitate credendi is the synthesis of his Manichean period and the route he had to follow until he reached the pure truth. Our science includes the things that we have seen, and those that, without seeing them, we believe. In the first case it is we ourselves who bear witness; In the second it is the testimony of others, whether oral or written, that determines our assent. The Augustinian formula: "Intellige ut credas; crede ut intelligas", seems contradictory if we do not take into account that the role of the intelligence that precedes faith is different from that of that which follows it. Before faith, intelligence is natural reason, and its object is not the content of faith, but the natural reasons we have for "eum assensione cogitare"; On the other hand, the object of the intelligence that follows faith is faith itself, it is the truth believed, which illuminates and transforms it, elevating it to the supernatural order. But this second function requires in the subject a minimum of conditions that are repugnant to the proud and demanding attitude of the Manichaeans and those who disdain the truth presented in the simple garb of the Old Testament. • In the very order of human things, faith is absolutely necessary; If we do not believe, if our faith is not protected by a stronghold of truths, even human life in society becomes impossible. Primary society, the one that is protected by the bonds of piety, the one that is woven with that treasure that is friendship, is impossible without faith, without a fiducial credit that impels us to accept what we are told without further rational disquisition. Before knowing a science it is necessary to accept, at least provisionally, the authority of a teacher; even more so in the religious order. Already in the book De ordine he had written five years earlier: "... to all those who wish to gain knowledge of the high and serious questions of culture, authority opens the door" (II, 9, 26). The te in Saint Augustine is at the same time, adhesion of the spirit to the supernatural truth and submissive abandonment of man to the grace of Christ.

That humility that implies the submission of the spirit to the authority of God and trust in Him, which is at the same time love and charity, purifies and illuminates the soul. This purification belongs to the conditions that make man capable of believing and, subsequently, understanding (I, 4). And that passage: The same veil continues over the lesson of the old covenant, without seeing that only through Christ has it been removed. It is not that Christ removes the Old Testament, but that he reveals it, so that through Christ what would become intelligible and patent that without it would remain dark and closed. Next line the Apostle himself says: But when they return to the Lord, the veil will be removed. It does not say that the law or even the Old Testament will be removed, as if they covered up useless things, but that the grace of the Lord will remove the veil that hides profitable things. This is, then, the way of proceeding of those who with pious zeal seek the meaning of the sacred Scriptures. The orderly succession of things is carefully shown, the reason for what is done or said and the admirable harmony between one testament and another, without leaving a single accent that discords the whole: the antitypes figured there are so evident that the difficulties that are resolved at the edge of interpretation force us to recognize the misfortune of those who dare to censure them without knowing them.

Without focusing for now on the profound problems of science, I am going to treat you as I think one should treat a friend, that is, according to my way of seeing and not as I have seen, full of admiration, that learned people do. There are three kinds of errors that can be made when reading something. I will talk about each of them. The first consists of taking what is false as true, even if the writer did not intend to take what is false as true. The second, although less widespread, no less harmful, is that what is false is taken for true, because the author of the writing also does so. When in reading truths are perceived that the author did not realize, the third error occurs. This third party contains many advantages; well thought out, the fruit of reading is complete. A case of the first kind would be the error of those who believe that Rhadamanthus sees and judges the causes of the dead in hell, because Virgil tells us so. The former's error would be twofold: he holds for certain what is false, and he also believes that this was the thought of the author he reads. The second error admits this exemplification: someone who, because Lucretius writes that souls are made up of atoms and that upon death they resolve into atoms and die, thought that they should accept it as true. His misfortune is no less considering that what is false is true, although Lucretius also participated in that false thought, in such an important matter. let her know. The latter think that they do not know her nor do they want to know her. Likewise, there are three operations in the soul that each seem to be a continuation of the other, and that it is convenient to discern: understand, believe and give an opinion. If they are considered in isolation, understanding is always free of all defects; the second admits some fault; the third has the logical consequence of imperfection. Understanding great, honest things, even divine things, constitutes the highest happiness; Understanding superfluous things does not cause any harm; dedicating himself to his study consumed the time perhaps necessary for other studies. Nor is there any harm to be feared from the mere fact of understanding what is evil; The unfortunate thing is to do it. Because if one understands how he can kill his enemy without danger to himself, the very act of understanding it, without the desire to carry it out, does not make him guilty; Lacking this desire, can there be anything more innocuous? On the other hand, there is guilt in believing something that goes against divine excellence and when one lightly believes something that goes against the dignity of some man. Whatever else you believe, if you understand that nothing is known about it, you are exempt from blame. Thus I believe that the most criminal among the conspirators were killed due to Cicero's courage; I have no knowledge of this fact, but I know that it is entirely impossible for me to know it. Suspicion is doubly shameful: first, because he who has persuaded himself that he knows something is incapable of instructing himself in that same thing, assuming that it is knowable; secondly, reckless judgment is a sign of a soul that is not well disposed, and thus, if someone thought he knew the same thing as what I just said about Cicero, even if no one prevented him from dedicating himself to his research, since it is about something that he cannot know with certainty, he would commit a real mistake, because he does not realize the great difference that exists between what can be known for a certain reason of the spirit and what is collected in writings or in oral tradition for the benefit of future generations, since that every error implies a deformity. Therefore, what we understand, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority; what we conjecture, to error. But all those who understand also believe, and those who conjecture believe; but not everyone who believes understands, and whoever conjectures does not understand.

A very difficult question now arises: how can the fool find the wise man, if the majority of men, although not directly, at least indirectly, apply to themselves the nickname of wise men, and if, furthermore, they are so discordant in their concepts of the things whose knowledge constitutes wisdom, that either none of them is wise or only one will truly be wise? I see no way that the fool can know him; because nothing can be known by certain signs, unless the thing itself is known by its external manifestations. Now a fool does not know wisdom. It is not wisdom like gold, silver or similar things, which when seen are known and remain external to the knower; Not so with wisdom, which cannot be seen with the eyes of the soul if it is not possessed. The objects perceptible by the senses are offered to us from outside, and it is possible to see things other than the eyes without them or others of the same kind being housed within us. But the objects of intellectual perception are within the soul: seeing them is in this case the same as possessing them. But the fool is devoid of wisdom, therefore he does not know what wisdom is. He cannot see it with his eyes; He cannot conceive it without possessing it, nor possess it and continue in his foolishness. He does not know her, and while he does not know her, he cannot know her anywhere. Therefore, there is no one who, being a fool, can, as long as he remains so, safely find the wise man to free himself, by obeying him, from the great evil that is foolishness. 29, Now, since our study has religion as its object, only God can provide a solution to this enormous difficulty; On the other hand, if we do not believe in its existence and its efficiency in helping the human mind, we should not logically seek true religion. 35. The influence of customs on the spirit of men is so great that it is easier to reprove and abhor the part of evil that is in them—generally residues of concupiscence—than to abandon and change them. Do you think that the fact that not only a few wise men defend that the worship due to God—whom can only be grasped with intelligence—should not be surrendered to anything earthly, neither of a fiery nature nor perceptible to the senses, but that the same mass of ignorant people, of peoples as numerous as they are different, believe so and so proclaim it is a small contribution to the interests of man? And is it not also continence that tolerates only a crumb of bread for every meal and prolonged fasts for several days, and chastity that does not take care of either marriage or children; the patience that has nothing in crosses or flames; the liberality that distributes his assets among the poor; the contempt, in short, for everything in this world, which makes death itself desirable? Few, it is true, are those who practice these things, even less are those who govern themselves with prudence when practicing them; but the people lend them their ears and their approval and veneration, and end up loving them. To demonstrate how it is possible that, not being God willing. has engendered or made evil, and that, since there is no nature or any substance that has not been engendered or made by Him, it nevertheless frees us from evil, reasons are adduced there that urge assent, that dispel all doubt, particularly for you and those of your same conscience, provided that the good nature is accompanied by a certain degree of piety and tranquility of spirit, essential to come to understand, even in part, such great things. This is not an unheedable rumor or some fable of Persian origin, which only requires a little attention and does not ask for any acute genius, but for childish intelligence. The truth behaves very differently from how the Manichaeans dream of it. But since this dissertation has gone on much longer than I had thought, I am finishing this book.

Do not lose sight of when reading it that I have not intended to refute the Manicheans with it or deal with these impostures, nor have I intended to present to you high concepts of the Catholic faith, but rather I have sought, as far as possible, to dispel the false idea about true Christians that they amass against us with no less clumsiness than malice, and at the same time awaken in you concern for great and divine things. This volume has thus been concluded. When your spirit is calmer, perhaps you will begin to discuss other topics.
